subject: Waterfront
text:
Maximize recreation, and make room for travel. That is the order. The waterfront’s first job is swimming, fishing, sailing, walking and the off-leash area, and a ferry has to fit around them. The City and the Water Emergency Transportation Authority (WETA), which runs San Francisco Bay Ferry, plan a new 1,080-foot pier with a breakwater and a ferry landing at its end, estimated at about $105 million. Construction is not funded. I support a battery-electric ferry to San Francisco, landing inside the Marina basin next to the hotel. The water there is already protected and already dredged for the boats in the Marina. Waterfront engineers I’ve met with estimate an in-Marina landing at about $20 million. Nobody has published a study of it, and the City has not done one. 

    Recreation first, then room for travel. Every decision below is judged by what it does for the people who use the waterfront now, and then by whether it makes room for a ferry. A ferry that takes the parking, the water or the quiet from recreation fails the first test.
    Land it inside the Marina, next to the hotel. Before the City commits to a $105 million pier and breakwater, it should price a landing in the basin, where the water is already protected and already dredged. If the in-Marina landing costs a fraction of the pier, that is the project.
    Yes to a battery-electric ferry. WETA is building its first battery-electric high-speed ferries now. No vessels have been assigned to the Berkeley route. The first condition is a written commitment that the route runs electric from the first day of service.
    WETA pays for the ferry. Its landing, the dredging it needs, and all operations, with no City operating subsidy. That is what the City said in 2021. It belongs in a signed agreement.
    Add it in steps. Start service with the parking that exists. Add sailings, and any ferry parking, only when ridership has met a target published in advance.
    Recreation parking stays free. Time limits of about six hours keep all-day commuters out of the spaces nearest the parks.
    The pier is its own question. In 2021 the City priced a recreation-only rebuild at $20 million to $55 million. With the ferry inside the Marina, the pier can be rebuilt for fishing and walking on its own budget and schedule.

subject: Budget
text:
Berkeley's adopted budget and its year-end books differ by tens of millions. Council should see the difference before every budget vote.
Each June the City Council adopts a General Fund budget. About six months after the fiscal year closes, the city publishes its audited Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR), which sets that budget beside what was actually collected and spent. For FY2024 and FY2025 the adopted budgets showed small surpluses. The year-end results showed drawdowns of $28.8 million and $16.7 million. Council adopted General Fund budgets showing a $3.9 million surplus for FY2024 and $2.0 million for FY2025. The city's own year-end schedules show the same budgets ended with drawdowns of $28.8 million and $16.7 million, measured the same way.
Part of that gap is money council approved in earlier years and carried forward. The rest is lines that run over every year, led by police and fire overtime: $11.8 million and $11.3 million above the adopted budget.
Money appropriated but neither spent nor put under contract by year-end tripled, from $41.2 million to $130.5 million. For three years running, the General Fund has also been covering an $11.7 to $13.1 million cash shortfall in the Grant Fund.
The budget-to-actual table is the one schedule the outside auditor gives no opinion on. Its expenditure variance carries the same small sign error three years in a row.
I'd put the audited budget-to-actual table, by department, on the agenda with every budget, and budget overtime at what it actually costs. results before it votes on next year's budget.

A budget is a forecast. Forecasts miss, and a miss is information. Berkeley already produces the record of every miss. It sits in a report of more than 300 pages, published about six months after the year closes. I'd make that record part of the budget vote, so the next forecast starts from what actually happened.

    Ask 01
    Put the audited budget-to-actual table on the agenda with every budget.

    Three years, by department, original budget, final budget and actual, with a written reason for every line more than 5% off its adopted figure. Publish it with the proposed budget. The city already prepares the numbers.
    Ask 02
    Budget police and fire overtime at what it has actually cost.

    Use the three-year actual as the starting figure. Report overtime monthly by department, with the vacancies it covered and mutual-aid costs billed and reimbursed. I found no published figure for mutual-aid reimbursement in the reports I reviewed.
    Ask 03
    Publish the carryover list every year.

    Every unspent appropriation carried forward: the project, the fund, the year it was first approved and the amount. Anything carried two years or more comes back to council for a vote to keep it.
    Ask 04
    Publish what other funds owe the General Fund.

    Each balance, how long it has been owed, and the date repayment is expected. Start with the $13.1 million in grant reimbursements, and name the grants.
    Ask 05
    Show the council action behind the FY2025 transfers.

    Transfers out of the General Fund ran $7.5 million above the final budget in FY2025, with no explanation in the report. If council authorized it, link the action from the city's budget page. If it didn't, say so.

To be clear about what this is not. Nothing in these reports suggests fraud. The outside auditor, Badawi & Associates, issued clean opinions both years and found no material weaknesses in internal control. Measured by standard accounting (GAAP), total General Fund balance held near $153 to $155 million. Spending money that council approved in an earlier year is legitimate, and it explains part of the gap.

This page doesn't blame police or fire. Overtime is what fills shifts when positions sit empty, and the city says so itself. The finance staff wrote the explanations quoted on this page. The asks are about what council sees and when it sees it.

subject: Housing
text:
Council adopted the San Pablo plan 9–0 on September 29. Its street work still has no cost and no payer.
The San Pablo Avenue Specific Plan rewrites what can be built along 1's main street: seven stories where four are allowed today, room for roughly 8,000 homes, and an estimated 20,000 new residents. I support the plan and the seven stories. The plan also promises wider sidewalks, street trees, lighting, crossings and side-street plazas, and it attaches no dollar figure to any of them and names no one to pay. The City Council adopted it 9–0 on September 29, five weeks before an election. The zoning ordinance gets its second reading on October 13. Yes to seven stories. Seven is the number the rest of the plan was built around: the environmental work, the street and utility assumptions, the estimate of roughly 8,000 homes. In June the Planning Commission turned down a motion to cut it to five, two votes to five, with one member absent. Ten stories appears nowhere in the City's record that I can find. Going taller from the dais would put the plan ahead of the work that was done to support it.
Keep the sixteen-foot sidewalk. The Planning Commission added it in June as a requirement, delivered by the builder through a ground-floor setback. It is the strongest public-realm provision in the plan. It should not be traded away at Council.
Put a number and a source on the street work. Council adopted the plan without one. The plan lists lighting, street trees, crossings, widened sidewalks and side-street plazas, and its funding chapter is a table of possible sources with checkmarks in boxes. Adopt a cost estimate and name the money.
Vote the repeals separately. The same resolution rescinds the West Berkeley Plan and the San Pablo Avenue Public Improvements Plan. Retiring the corridor's own improvements plan in the same breath as adopting a plan with no funded improvements is exactly the kind of bundling that should have been pulled apart. On September 29 it was not.
Count what gets delivered. The plan already promises annual progress reports. Have them report square feet of plaza, feet of widened sidewalk and trees planted against a target set in advance. If the incentives produce no plazas in three years, that is the evidence for turning them into requirements.

subject: Ballot Measures
text:
No on U, V and Z.
Seven local measures are on the November 3 ballot and four of them are taxes. I am voting no on three: the $300 million bond, the half-cent sales tax, and the parcel tax for a public bank. I am voting yes on three, and I am taking no position on the arts parcel tax. I do measurement and verification for a living — thirty years of answering one question for building owners, which is whether the money delivered what was promised. Every one of these three fails that question in a different way, and the failures are in the city’s own documents rather than anybody’s campaign literature. No on three.
Yes on three.
Neutral on one.

I want to be exact about what this is not. It is not an anti-tax position: I am voting yes on three measures on this same ballot, one of which is a tax. It is not a claim that Berkeley’s needs are exaggerated — the city’s own auditor puts unfunded capital and deferred maintenance at $1.8 billion, which is worse than most residents think. And it is not an accusation against staff, who wrote what they were asked to write.

It is a claim about instruments. A bond that lists thirty-one projects and commits to none, with no operating budget for what it builds. A general tax that makes no promise and never ends. A parcel tax for an institution that has no charter and a written contingency for what happens to the money if it never gets one. In my working life, if a client brought me any of these three and asked whether the savings were real, the answer would be that the question cannot be answered as written. I am not willing to vote yes on something I could not later verify.

Berkeley requires measurement and verification before it pays an energy contractor — measured outcomes, against a defensible baseline, under international protocols. The city applies that standard to a $2 million retrofit. It does not apply it to a $300 million bond.
ASK 01
Publish the prioritized project list and the Program Plan update, then come back for the bond.

Berkeley already has a Program Plan — the Council adopted it on July 26, 2022, with $1.802 billion in needs and six targets. What it does not have is a year on any of those targets, or the updated plan the Mayor’s Task Force set for spring 2026, which I have not been able to locate. Publish the update — the asset baseline, the sequence, the funding path for the rest — alongside the thirty-one projects ranked in order, and a $300 million bond stops being a menu and becomes step one of something. I would vote for that bond and say so in writing. I set this out in full on the Vision 2050 page, where my answer is yes to the plan: date the targets and publish the score.
ASK 02
Both price tags on the same ballot.

Every capital measure states what the finished thing costs to operate, and where that money comes from. Measure C did this in 2010 and Berkeley has not done it since. A building the city cannot afford to staff is not an asset; it is a liability with a ribbon on it.
ASK 03
A baseline and a target, in measurable units, in the ballot language.

Not “street repair.” Lane-miles brought to a stated pavement condition index at a stated cost, by a stated date. A purpose is what a measure is for. A boundary is what it promises. Voters can only hold the second one to account.
ASK 04
An annual report of outcome against target — not only of dollars spent.

Measures U and Z both already require an audit at least every three years and an annual report. I want to be fair about that: it is real, and it is more than nothing. But an audit confirms the money went where it was supposed to go. It does not say whether the streets got smoother or the loans got made. Add one column — what we said we would achieve, what we achieved — and the reports become worth reading.
ASK 05
An escalator that pauses when targets are missed.

Twenty-nine assessments rise automatically whether or not they deliver, and Measure Z would add a thirtieth that rises with inflation with no stated way for Council to pause it. Tie the escalator to the annual report: miss the target, the increase waits until the next report shows it met. This is ordinary practice in performance contracting and it is the highest-leverage line on this page.
ASK 06
Fix the twenty-nine before adding the thirtieth.

The structural deficit is real — the City Auditor projects $32 million in FY2027 and $33 million in FY2028 — and voting no does not make it disappear. I am not pretending otherwise. But the escalator asymmetry on the existing bill is a larger revenue story than half a cent of sales tax, and nobody is working on it. That is work I would do.

subject: Infrastructure
text:
Berkeley adopted infrastructure targets in 2022. The streets still score 56.
Vision 2050 is Berkeley's 30-year plan for its streets, sidewalks, sewers, storm drains, parks and public buildings. Voters called for it in 2018, when Measure R passed with 85 percent, and the Council adopted its framework in 2020. I support it. In 2022 the Council adopted a Program Plan with real targets: a pavement score above 70, the sidewalk repair backlog finished, and the bicycle and pedestrian plans fully built. None of those targets has a year attached. Berkeley's streets scored 56 in 2022 and 56 again in 2024, the latest year published. The Task Force's own report last December gave no progress figures for them. Yes to the plan. Vision 2050 asks the City to run its streets, pipes and buildings the way a careful owner would: know what it owns, know what condition it is in, repair it before it fails, dig up a street once, and double capital spending to about $80 million a year. That is the discipline of my profession, and I would hold the City to it.
Put a year on each target. The 2022 plan says: "The target is to improve Berkeley's streets to a PCI of more than 70." It gives no year. Neither do the targets for sidewalks or for the bicycle and pedestrian plans. Without a year, nobody can say whether the City is on schedule.
Publish the score every year. One page, released with the budget: each target, this year's figure, and last year's. The street score already exists, because the Metropolitan Transportation Commission publishes it every year. The Task Force itself called for annual progress reports.
Finish what the Task Force scheduled. The Task Force says condition assessments have started and the City's asset management software is "fully implemented." The first public product should be the condition of each class of asset: streets, sidewalks, sewers, storm drains and buildings.
Measure U is a separate decision. The City's staff report for the $300 million bond on the November ballot says project prioritization "will continue to be guided by the Vision 2050 framework." Whether to vote for Measure U is its own question, and it gets its own page.

subject: Golden Gate Fields
text:
Golden Gate Fields becomes a park. Nobody has published what it costs to open.
The former racetrack on the Albany–Berkeley shoreline is being bought for $175 million and handed to the East Bay Regional Park District. It is 161 acres, and about 40 of them are in Berkeley, inside 1. I support the park. The purchase price covers the land and the removal of the buildings. It does not cover the cleanup, the construction of a park, or the cost of running one, and none of those numbers has been published. Berkeley has also not said what it loses in taxes when the land goes off the rolls. Albany has. Yes to the park. A continuous public shoreline from Richmond to Oakland has been the goal for decades. The Park set aside $20 million for this site in Measure WW in 2008 and named it in its 2013 Master Plan. Berkeley pays nothing toward the purchase, and the Park will own, run and pay to maintain the site.
Publish the cost to open it. The $175 million buys the land with the buildings removed. The cleanup cost is unknown. The Park says development will come in phases "beyond 2029" as money is found. A public process that starts without a cost range is planning without a budget.
Berkeley should publish what it loses. Once a public agency owns the land, it stops paying property tax. Albany published its figures in May: about $1.1 million a year to the city and $700,000 to its school district. Berkeley's figure for its 40 acres is a number the Council should have in front of it.
Open it in the meantime. The Park says it will look for interim uses. The obvious one is parking for the Tom Bates fields and Albany Beach, and the Bay Trail stays open. I'd want the interim plan written down, with what "secured for safety" means for public access.
The grandstand is open. Whether to tear down the old racetrack buildings or study reusing them is a real argument, and I have not taken a side. Both cases are further down this page, along with what each side would have to show.

subject: Surveillance
text:
Berkeley never put its surveillance contract out to bid.
Not once. Not in 2021, when a Council referral named Flock Safety before any evaluation had happened. Not in 2023, when the contract was awarded. Not in 2025, when the cameras were added. And not in 2026, when the City proposed spending roughly $2 million more with the same company.

Most of the argument about Flock in Berkeley has been about surveillance. That argument is worth having. But it has crowded out a simpler question that the Police Accountability Board and the City Auditor have both now put on the record: did the City follow its own purchasing rules? The answer appears to be no — and that is a problem I can actually fix from a Council seat.  I am not going to tell you license plate readers are useless. Los Angeles audited two months of its own system and found 337 vehicle recoveries and 74 felony arrests. That is real. I am also not going to tell you they reduce crime, because fifteen years of independent research says they don't — they help solve some crimes after the fact, which is a smaller and more honest claim than the one being sold to us.

What I will say is this: a city that cannot show its work on a $2 million surveillance purchase has no business asking residents to trust it with the cameras. Verification first. That applies to energy savings, it applies to budgets, and it applies here.

    Ask 01
    Competitive RFP before any renewal or expansion.

    No new contract, extension, or letter of intent with any surveillance vendor until BPD publishes written functional requirements and the City runs a real solicitation. This is the PAB's own recommendation, adopted unanimously on April 22, 2026.
    Ask 02
    Make competitive procurement binding, not advisory.

    Berkeley's Municipal Code does not legally require competition for service contracts — the rules live in a policy manual with no enforcement teeth. The City Auditor recommended closing that gap. I would carry that ordinance. It fixes every future contract, not just this one.
    Ask 03
    Publish the access-log audits. All of them.

    Monthly audits, semiannual published reports, sent to the PAB. Elsewhere, misuse has been found by journalists and litigants rather than by internal review. Assume ours will need outside eyes too, and design for it.
    Ask 04
    Match the terms Oakland and Richmond already got.

    Penalties of $200,000–$290,000 per violation, no carve-out for lookup tools, no federal task-force loophole, and full legal remedies preserved where actual harm exceeds the penalty. Flock accepted these terms next door. There is no reason Berkeley should take less.
    Ask 05
    Report outcomes with denominators.

    "120+ arrests and leads" is not a number anyone can evaluate. Report arrests, charges filed, and cases cleared as separate counts against total alerts and total false alerts. If the system is working, the real numbers will show it.

To be clear about what this is not

This is not a proposal to rip out the 52 existing cameras, and it is not a claim that BPD acted in bad faith. A department under authorized strength reaching for a tool that promises to multiply its capacity is a predictable response to a real staffing problem. The failure here is procedural, it belongs to the City's process rather than to any individual, and process is exactly what a Council seat is for.

subject: Zoning
text:
Corridor upzoning: keep the neighborhoods we already have.
SB 79 took effect July 1, 2026. AB 893 took effect January 1. AB 2011 has applied to every commercial corridor since 2023. The minimum heights near BART, near campus, and along San Pablo and University are no longer the Council's to set. What the Council still controls is narrower, more technical, and mostly not being done: the design standards, the feasibility math, the tenant rules, and whether anyone measures what gets built. Keep the neighborhoods. Write the standards first. Count what gets built.

I am for the neighborhoods 1 already has. Where the state has set the floor — San Pablo, University, near BART — the Council's remaining job is to make sure what gets built fits the street it lands on, and the only lawful way left to do that is objective design standards in place before the applications arrive. Where the state has set no floor — Solano and College, and North Shattuck above the SB 79 line — I would vote against the added heights. And I am against pretending that a zoning map is a housing program.

My job for twenty-five years has been checking whether claimed results were real. Every one of the asks below is a verification step the City is currently skipping.

    Ask 01
    Add shadow, wind and street-tree rules to San Pablo's objective design standards — before the applications arrive.

    The design standards were adopted with the plan on September 29. The Public Review Draft's Appendix E had none of the three, and I have not confirmed that the adopted version added any. North Berkeley BART's standards already require one street tree per 25 feet of sidewalk; use them. Write graduated standards — a maximum share of a plaza newly shaded — not absolute bans, so they survive AB 2011's "reasonable and broadly applicable" test. Once an application is filed, it's over.
    Ask 02
    No added heights on Solano, College, or North Shattuck above the state floor.

    No state floor applies on Solano or College, and SB 79 reaches North Shattuck only at its southern end. On those blocks what the Council adopts is the whole outcome. By the plan's own density caps, the Opportunity Sites option puts a nine-story bonus building on Solano and ten stories on North Shattuck — on two- and three-story shopping streets. I'd vote no on the added heights, and yes to housing that fits the base standards already on the books.
    Ask 03
    No corridor vote without a published pro forma.

    The Terner Center publishes the method. Run it on a typical San Pablo and Solano parcel at the proposed height, with Berkeley's 20% inclusionary and 2026 costs. If it doesn't pencil, the rezoning raises land prices and produces nothing — what happened in Chicago. If it does, say so with numbers and the debate gets shorter.
    Ask 04
    Measure units built, not units permitted — and publish nearby rents.

    The Rent Board's registry lets Berkeley run the UC Berkeley rent studies on its own blocks. An annual corridor look-back: permits, completions, occupancy, and registry rents within 250 meters of each finished building. Downtown (2012) and Southside (2023) are ready-made test cases the City has never measured.
    Ask 05
    Put tenant and small-business protections in the ordinance text, not the staff report.

    The City's own commissioned study found West Berkeley lost 31% of its BIPOC residents and saw rents rise $1,814 a month from 2009 to 2019, and recommended steering upzoning away from West and South Berkeley. The finding is real. Where state law has already fixed the height, the protections have to do the work: one-for-one replacement, relocation, pre-application tenant notice and tax relief for displaced businesses should be binding.
    Ask 06
    A fiscal-impact line in every corridor staff report — including the cost of serving it.

    Assessed-value and property-tax effect at 25%, 50% and 100% build-out over ten years, net of the cost of serving the new residents. The City has never published one for a rezoning. Every upzoning is sold partly as a budget fix; put the number on the table so the claim can be checked, and so nobody trades a neighborhood for revenue that never arrives.
    Ask 07
    Stop litigating what Sacramento already decided.

    Hearings spent arguing about SB 79 heights near BART are hearings not spent on the six things the Council can still shape. I'd vote against spending staff time on an SB 79 exemption ordinance unless staff can show a parcel-specific legal basis.

To be clear about what this is not

This is not opposition to housing on San Pablo or University — the state has settled that those corridors get taller, and the fight there is over the standards. It is not a promise that corridor housing will make Berkeley affordable. The lower-income share of the City's target — 5,270 units — is not going to come from upzoning; it comes from inclusionary units and subsidized construction, and the City has permitted 4% of it. Anyone telling you a zoning map solves that is selling something.

subject: Homelessness
text:
Berkeley controls 56 of the 320 shelter beds inside Berkeley.
The county controls referrals to the other 264. The city's main homelessness fund is projected to go below zero this year and $22.8 million below zero by 2029. And the department that runs all of it cannot tell you its own vacancy rate, because nobody publishes one. Measure it. Then fund it.

Some of this clearly works. Berkeley has won three state Encampment Resolution grants — People's Park, the Harrison Street corridor, Second and Cedar — worth about $15 million. Those motel rooms, together with the Measure P–funded beds at the Berkeley Inn, are the 56 the Auditor counted as city-controlled: filled by Berkeley's own outreach teams rather than the county queue. And since February 2026 a newer program, CareBridge, has added 30 rooms at the Signature Inn under an $8 million state grant — "a no-match grant with no impact on the City's General Fund" — where Berkeley police identify candidates and the provider screens and admits them, also outside the county queue. (CareBridge is a post-arrest diversion program; the city is explicit that "being unhoused is not the criteria.") These are real results, won by staff who wrote good applications — one was declined once, and they went back.

But a city spending $25 million a year should be able to hand a resident one table showing where it went and what came back. Until it can, every allocation vote is a vote taken on faith. I'm not asking to cut it. I'm asking what it bought. Five asks — each one a report, not a program:

    Ask 01
    One table, every site: who pays, who refers, who got in.

    For each shelter, motel and supportive-housing site the city funds — the funding source, who controls referrals (city, county Coordinated Entry, or the provider), and the share of placements in the last twelve months who were Berkeley residents. The Auditor already built the bed count. Finish the table.
    Ask 02
    A five-year Measure P sustainability table before the next allocation vote.

    The fund goes negative on the City Manager's own numbers, and the Homeless Services Panel of Experts recommends allocations one year at a time. Council should not allocate FY2028 money without seeing FY2028–2032 revenue under three housing-market scenarios, and what each program is funded at when the transfer tax comes in at FY2024 levels.
    Ask 03
    One HHCS outcomes dashboard that both three-year plans report into.

    Pick ten numbers — shelter exits to permanent housing, crisis calls resolved without transport, time-to-fill for clinicians — and publish them quarterly against both plans. If the CHIP and the BHSA plan cannot share a single baseline, they are not coordinating. They are coexisting.
    Ask 04
    Vacancy and time-to-fill, by division, every quarter.

    The Auditor flagged a 19% citywide vacancy rate in 2023, second-highest of the nine Bay Area cities it compared. Three years on, the city still publishes one number for roughly 1,560 positions. Break it out by department and division, with the median days a posted position stays open. You cannot plan a service around staff you cannot count.
    Ask 05
    Bring the contracts ordinance to a vote — and make it cover amendments.

    The proposed amendment to BMC 7.18 would require competitive solicitation above $100,000. It was referred to the Budget & Finance Committee on 27 April 2026 and has not reached Council; the July meeting it was scheduled for was cancelled. It needs two additions: an amendment that pushes a contract past the threshold should trigger the same rule, and the annual report should be a standing Council item rather than a records request.

To be clear about what this is not

This is not an argument to cut Measure P, close a shelter, or sweep anyone. Berkeley voters passed Measure P with 72% and Measure W with 61%; that purpose is legitimate and I will defend it. My standard on encampments is the same one I apply everywhere else on this site: no closure without a documented offer of placement, and published 30- and 90-day outcomes for the people who were there.

It is also not an accusation against HHCS staff or against any provider. I have not found, and do not assert, that a particular contract was awarded improperly or that a particular program underperforms. The claim is narrower and, I think, harder to argue with: this is a system nobody measures end to end.

subject: Health
text:
In June 2026, Berkeley adopted a three-year behavioral-health plan carrying about $36 million in state money. I read it looking for one thing: a target — any number the city promises to hit, with a baseline and a date. I could not find one. Neither could I find a council discussion: the plan passed on the consent calendar, with no item-specific debate, in a single vote alongside routine contracts. This page is about the difference between counting what we spend and measuring what it does. None of this is an accusation. The community process behind the BHSA plan was real — meetings, a comment period, a public hearing. The staff who wrote it followed the state's template. And where Berkeley has measured, the results look good: those FSP numbers are the kind every program should have to show. The failure is structural, and it belongs to the council level: nobody on the dais has ever debated what Berkeley itself should measure.

The city measures activity — dollars allocated, people served — at scale, and measures outcomes only where the state forces it, on cohorts of a few dozen. Every ask below is a report, not a program.
ASK 01
Publish Berkeley's own targets for the BHSA plan before its first annual update.

The state template gives us six goal areas. Berkeley should say the numbers: for each of the plan's three buckets — housing interventions, Full Service Partnerships, services and supports — a baseline, a target, and a date. If staff already track these internally, publishing costs nothing. If they don't, that's worth knowing before year two of three.
ASK 02
Fill in Appendix C — or say why it's still blank.

The CHIP promised its performance measures during "phase 1 of Implementation," which ended around March 2026, and promised an annual progress report with community updates every six months. Publish the completed appendix and the first progress report, or publish the reason they don't exist.
ASK 03
Scale the scorecard the city already knows how to build.

The MHSA update proves Berkeley can track hospitalizations, jail days, and follow-up rates for 66 people. Require the same outcome categories from every behavioral-health services contract above the bid threshold — as a reporting condition in the contract, the way the money already requires invoices.
ASK 04
Multi-year plans get a hearing at council — not just a consent vote.

Any plan committing more than $10 million across multiple years should be presented and discussed on the dais before adoption. A commission hearing is necessary; it is not sufficient. The BHSA plan got a community process and a consent vote. The one thing it never got was a council conversation.
ASK 05
One outcomes night a year, for the whole department.

The MHSA annual update was a discussion item in July 2025 — the pattern already exists. Make it standing: one council meeting a year where HHCS reports against the published measures for both plans, on ten numbers that don't change year to year. On the homelessness page I ask for a shared dashboard; this is where it gets read aloud.
ASK 06
Put the four commissions in one room, once a year.

Housing Advisory, Homeless Services Panel of Experts, Behavioral Health, Community Health — each reviews a slice of the same money for overlapping populations, and no body sees the whole. A joint annual session over one shared table — every housing-for-health dollar, its source, its reviewing body, its measure — before the Panel makes its Measure P recommendations and before the BHSA annual update. It costs an evening. And fill the vacant seats first.
To be clear about what this is not

This is not a claim that Berkeley's behavioral-health programs fail — where the city measured, the results were good news. It is not an attack on HHCS staff, on the commissioners who held the hearings, or on the community members who showed up in February and April. It is not an argument to cut the money: the state set these allocations and Berkeley should spend every dollar. The claim is narrower and documented: a city can't tell whether $36 million worked if it never wrote down what "worked" means. Council hasn't asked. I will.

subject: Accountability
text:
Between September 2026 and June 2027, five dated decisions will settle how many shelter beds Berkeley keeps, what happens to $14.9 million the city transferred but never programmed, and whether the contracting fix the Auditor asked for ever becomes law. None of them will be framed as "the homelessness debate." All of them are the homelessness debate.  Nothing on this page alleges misspending. The behavioral-health plan's arithmetic foots to the penny — I checked. What it shows instead is a planning gap: money moved on paper but not programmed, promises made in one document while the budget cut their foundations in another, and expiring grants with no named successor. Those are fixable, and each has a scheduled moment where fixing it is one motion.

    Ask 01 · at the BHSA Annual Update
    Program the $14.9 million — or publish the reason for holding it.

    The plan's own budget tables transfer $18,193,420 of unspent MHSA funds into the three new components, then program only the legally dedicated ~$3.3 million. Housing receives $4.5 million of the transfer and budgets zero of it. A revenue hedge may be defensible — the state fund swings 30% with capital-gains years — but a hedge you never state is just idle money during a shelter shortage. Say which it is, in the update, in writing.
    Ask 02 · before the Measure P fund allocation vote
    A five-year sustainability table, published first.

    The City Manager's own memo projects the Measure P fund from +$5.6 million in FY24 to −$22.8 million in FY29 under current allocations. And because Measure P is legally a general tax, its "fund" is a policy ledger, not a lockbox — a negative balance doesn't pause the spending, it quietly shifts the gap onto the same General Fund that carries the citywide deficit. The advisory panel and Council should see, on one page, what each allocation level does to that trajectory under a weak, base, and strong housing market — before voting, not after.
    Ask 03 · at the FY28 budget update
    A named successor for every expiring dollar.

    The record on this page shows four funding streams dying in sequence: the state grant for shelter operations (already expired, December 2025), the interim-housing money behind the $6.85 million cliff (by 2028), the encampment wellness project's innovation funds (exhausted during FY 2028-29), and the opioid-settlement line (zero after FY28). Each one gets a named successor source or a stated end-of-service date. No silent expirations.
    Ask 04 · at Budget & Finance, October 5
    Pass the contracting fix — with a reporting requirement attached.

    The proposed BMC 7.18 amendment would finally require competitive solicitation for service contracts over $100,000. It should also cover amendments — the Auditor found contracts that started under $50,000 and grew by an average of $218,000 — and require an annual public report. If it stalls again, that is itself a finding.
    Ask 05 · in every plan, every year
    One baseline, one target, one date, per program.

    The three-year behavioral-health plan contains projected headcounts and not a single numeric target. The city already collects the baselines; it just never connects them to a promise. And to be precise about what gets measured:
    targets belong on systems and money
    — dollars programmed, beds funded, response times, contracts competed, tenancies retained —
    not quotas on human beings
    . Badly chosen metrics push programs toward the easiest, most compliant clients; that is an argument for choosing metrics well, not for having none. This is the subject of its own page — Where's the scorecard? — and it is the condition I would attach to every annual update I vote on.

To be clear about what this is not

This is not a claim that anyone misspent a dollar, and not a proposal to cut these programs. It is a schedule. Cities reveal their priorities on consent calendars and committee agendas, in months when nobody is watching. The dates marked (expected) are estimates from the city's own prior cycles and are corrected here the day an agenda posts. If I have a date or a number wrong, tell me and the page changes.

subject: Bike Lanes
text:
On July 28, 2026, the City Council picked protected bike lanes on Hopkins Street — concrete-separated lanes running from The Alameda to the Ohlone Greenway — as the design Berkeley will build when the street is repaved. I would not have voted for it. There was a second option that night: work up a real bike route on Ada and Rose instead, then lay the two side by side and pick the better one. That's the one I'd have voted for. It would have delayed nothing — Hopkins isn't due for repaving until 2027–28 — and it lost by a single vote.  No on the Hopkins bike lane design. Yes on comparing it to the other route first. Berkeley has two plausible ways to connect North and West Berkeley by bike: Hopkins itself, or a route a few blocks over on Ada and Rose. Councilmember Brent Blackaby, co-sponsored by Councilmember Bartlett, moved to have staff work the Ada/Rose route up properly and lay both options side by side before the city committed to either. It would not have delayed the repaving or the bike lanes by a single day, because Hopkins isn't due for repaving until 2027–28. It lost by one vote. Berkeley declined to spend zero extra days finding out whether the other route was better. That's the vote I'd want back.

    That vote mattered more than my own preference — and the difference is the whole point. If you ask what I'd build, I'd repave Hopkins properly, stripe painted bike lanes, and put real money into traffic enforcement. But that's a preference, and a preference shouldn't win just because the person holding it got elected. The Ada/Rose motion wasn't "my design instead of theirs." It was show both, then choose — and I'd have voted for it knowing the comparison might come back against me.
    Why I'd have voted no on the main motion, reason one: nobody can tell you what it costs. The Council item priced it at $14–15 million against roughly $11 million for pedestrian-and-paving improvements alone; accounts of the meeting put the total as high as $20 million. There is no engineered design behind those numbers. I don't vote for a six-million-dollar spread on a street that could be repaved and striped now.
    Reason two: the tradeoffs were named and never quantified. Fire needs travel-lane width and response speed; a raised crosswalk slows an engine and the city calls that "a pragmatic trade-off" without saying by how many seconds; seniors need the curb at the door; the hills behind the corridor need evacuation capacity, assessed by a study still written in the future tense. Every one of those is real. Not one has a number attached.
    Reason three: the process has holes I can't explain away. Berkeley's own Complete Streets Policy has required before-and-after measurement and an annual report to Council since 2012, and I could find no such report published. The author of the 2018 referral said staff delivered a narrower study than she asked for. A three-year pause happened by City Manager memo rather than Council vote, with two different reasons given. Details are further down this page.
    What I am not saying. I'm not anti-bike, and I'm not disputing the safety problem. The city's record counts 46 pedestrian and bicycle crashes on Hopkins from 2011 to 2026, three of them fatal. The amendment I'd have backed would not have stopped a bike lane from being built — it would have made the city look at a second route first. Anyone who tells you this was safety versus no safety is selling something.
    Why I'm putting this in writing. The safe move is to call the vote done and talk about something else — and you'd never know what I thought until I was already in the seat. You're entitled to know how someone would have voted before you decide whether to give them a vote.
    And where I am now: waiting for the design phase, and not pretending to know how it ends. The engineering, the real cost, the Fire Department's findings and the evacuation study are all still ahead, and they will either firm this project up or open it back up. I'm not going to promise you an outcome I can't deliver. If it proceeds, I'll work to balance the effects on the people who carry them — the merchants, the drivers who can no longer park at the door, the seniors and disabled residents who need that curb. If it comes back open, the alternative gets the same scrutiny I'm asking of this one.

subject: Policing
text:
On September 29, 2026, the City Council voted 4 to 5 against Councilmember Kesarwani's resolution returning tear gas to the Police Department's Special Response Team and ending the pandemic-era moratorium on smoke and pepper spray. Packaged as one item, it makes three separable decisions — who can use CS gas (the chemical agent commonly called tear gas) and under what standard, what returns to crowd settings, and how each use gets reported afterward. Each carries different stakes, and the text of each is public.  The July version of this resolution is better drafted than the January version: it defines its terms, attaches its policies, and schedules its reports — much of what the Public Safety Committee conditioned its approval on. What remains is the difference between limits that read well and limits that bind. Every ask below is a number, a definition, or a report — nothing more — and each can be written into any new version without reopening 2020.

    Ask 01 · before any new vote
    The operational case, in numbers.

    Publish the count: how many Special Response Team incidents since June 2020 would have met this resolution's own critical-incident standard? The written record offers three examples in about 25 years, two of them in crowd settings the new text bars. If the count is substantial, publishing it makes the case better than any speech. If it is near zero, Council should know that before authorizing, and voters should know it before November.
    Ask 02 · in the operative text
    Close the crowd seam.

    Tear gas for crowd control is barred absolutely; smoke and OC return to crowds where there is "active violence." The threshold for that phrase should live in the resolution itself, alongside the Police Accountability Board's own words — First Amendment–protected activity excluded "without exception" — so the seam between a critical incident and a crowd can't be walked through in the moment.
    Ask 03 · reporting with consequences
    A missed report suspends the tool.

    The text promises a written report per use, quarterly reports to the PAB, annual reports to Council, and the state-required public summary. Add one sentence: if a deployment's report isn't published on schedule, the authorization is suspended until it is. I ask the same of the surveillance contracts — failure to publish should be automatic expiration, not a footnote.
    Ask 04 · a sunset with data attached
    Expire it unless renewed on the record.

    Authorization sunsets after two years unless Council renews it with the full usage record published — every deployment, every report, on time. If the tool is used as narrowly as promised, renewal is a consent-calendar formality. If it isn't, the sunset is the safeguard working.
    Ask 05 · mutual aid, both directions
    Berkeley's rules travel with Berkeley's officers — and bind its guests.

    The only deployment since 2014 in the resolution's record happened in Oakland, as mutual aid. And in 2014, assisting agencies stood on Telegraph alongside BPD. Write both directions into the mutual-aid policy: BPD operating elsewhere carries Berkeley's limits; outside agencies operating in Berkeley follow them; both get reported through the same scheme.
    Ask 06 · staff the referee
    Oversight on paper isn't oversight.

    The reporting scheme names the Police Accountability Board as its reviewer — in a year when two of the board's most experienced members resigned and the Director of Police Accountability was dismissed. Fill the seats and the director's office before the first quarterly report comes due. A safeguard that reports to an empty room isn't one.

To be clear about what this is not

The resolution's ban on tear gas for crowd control is absolute, and this page says so plainly. Special Response Team officers face real life-threatening incidents, and the critical-incident definition describes real ones. This is not a relitigation of 2020. It is a request that limits drafted well be made enforceable — thresholds in the operative text, reporting with consequences, a sunset with data, mutual aid covered. Council voted the September 29 version down, 4 to 5. If a new version returns with these in its text, it should get a vote on its merits. If I have a date or a clause wrong, tell me and the page changes.

subject: Surveillance
text:
Didn't Berkeley pass strong privacy protections to regulate Flock?

Sort of. Berkeley tried its best to have both surveillance and privacy. There are a few reasons I don't think it was enough.

    No enforcement mechanism. The privacy policies council passed are unenforceable — they depend on trusting Flock to abide by them. Our own Police Accountability Board reviewed the contract and found no legally enforceable way to hold Flock to anything. And there's a clear pattern of Flock disregarding the cities it works for: it installed cameras in Cambridge after being ordered to remove them, silently switched on nationwide access in Mountain View, and the ACLU has documented Flock repeatedly misleading city councils about who can reach the data.

    Police Accountability Board
    Cambridge Day — Dec 10, 2025

    Patterns of abuse and misuse. In August 2026 the Washington Post found at least 50 officers charged or accused of misusing plate readers — Flock's system in 46 cases, and in 26 of them to track wives, girlfriends, and ex-partners. Senator Wyden has told the FTC that Flock doesn't require basic multi-factor authentication, leaving the data open to hackers. No rule Berkeley writes fixes that.

    Longreads — Aug 3, 2026
    Office of Senator Ron Wyden — Nov 1, 2025

    Complicity in a dangerous project. Surveillance is a tool of authoritarians everywhere. Trump has sent the National Guard and ICE into American communities. He cheered on an insurrection and time and again ignored court rulings. If this administration decides it ‘needs’ access to this data, do we really believe it will stop to read Berkeley’s municipal code?

subject: Homelessness
text:
On Homelessness: Public Health, Not Tough on Crime

The status quo is awful and is not compassionate for anyone. Egregious income inequality and heartbreaking poverty contribute to a growing homelessness crisis throughout our region. It's hard to reconcile living in one of the wealthiest regions in the world with watching encampments grow and conditions worsen. People are right to be furious with those who have allowed this to continue, but we must be clear-eyed and honest about the role the City of Berkeley should take and what results we can expect.

West Berkeley has carried a disproportionate share of this crisis. Time and again, Districts 1 and 2 have borne the brunt of it; and while every part of the city needs to do what it can, West Berkeley cannot use this as a reason to stop helping. 

Berkeley cannot solve poverty or homelessness, and a tough-on-crime approach only serves to hide the problem. Even if we successfully removed all encampments and cleared every sidewalk, the people living on the streets would only be pushed to another sidewalk, another city, or into a carceral system that perpetuates poverty and is exorbitantly expensive for taxpayers. We need to accept that poverty is a problem whether it's in Berkeley, Richmond, or Santa Rita Jail.

We need to invest resources to combat the root causes of homelessness. As a city, we should focus on building more housing, improving access to physical and mental health care, providing quality education, and ensuring food and rental assistance. Housing First programs in particular are proven to keep people housed.¹ We also need to advocate for our state and federal governments to step up and create large-scale change, because anything Berkeley does alone will be a drop in the bucket.

We need to treat homelessness as a public health emergency. This means cleaning up and preventing hazardous large-scale encampments that endanger both their residents and the surrounding community, and working every day to get people off the streets and into housing. We need to open an emergency Alternative Sites shelter as soon as realistically possible and connect people with county resources. We also need to avoid punitive measures, such as citations and arrests, that do nothing to get people off the street, cost a fortune to enforce, increase liability risk, and only serve to move homelessness, not solve it.

We need to be honest about our limitations as a city and not mislead people with false solutions. We cannot solve poverty in Berkeley, and we also cannot and should not just push it out of the city. Living with and bearing witness to income inequality is a reality of the world we've created. I will work every day to bring our community together and search for creative, compassionate, and effective solutions.

We need to be both realistic and ambitious in our relentless pursuit of solutions to homelessness. I hope this summary helps people understand the current state of things and where I stand. More ideas about solutions are always welcome! Reach out to dariaforberkeley@proton.me with suggestions.

    Why criminalizing homelessness, even for people who refuse services, is bad public policy

    We have heard the suggestion for a policy to first connect people with social services, but if people refuse, cite, arrest, or forcibly remove them from city sidewalks.

    While this policy may sound common sense, it is not an honest or effective approach.

        Berkeley policy already states that the city can enforce state and local laws, which can include citation or arrest, if encampments create a hazard or nuisance for the public; this policy is enforceable regardless of the city's ability to offer housing.² In 2024, the council specifically named the Harrison Corridor as a priority for this enforcement,² and it has been enforced at city parks, such as Ohlone Park.³

        We have very little shelter to offer. Our congregate shelters have about 320 beds, while our homeless population was counted at 880 this year.⁴ Other options, such as motel rooms, are generally reserved for specific populations and are also at capacity. While motel rooms can offer high-quality, immediate shelter, in our current budget climate this is not a sustainable option. The city has already spent roughly $5 million leasing rooms for Harrison Street encampment residents.⁵ Given that budget crisis, the supply of empty shelter beds is likely to get worse.

        Citations against people who cannot pay generally become delinquent fines and can eventually become arrest warrants.⁶ This is how criminalization can trap people in cycles of poverty, and it's why Alameda County runs a program that dismisses tickets and fines for formerly homeless people.⁷

        When the only ‘crime’ being committed is homelessness, police enforcement uses up resources and offers a false sense of resolution. Very few people arrested for municipal camping violations are charged with actual crimes. The Attorney gets to decide how they prioritize enforcement, and in San Francisco, nearly 4 out of 5 people arrested for camping on the street were not charged.⁸ This means even if police increased enforcement, it would drive up costs without ever solving the problem. 

        A growing body of research shows that repeatedly and forcibly moving people from sidewalk to sidewalk poses serious public health risks and can lead to increased fatalities.⁹
    Homelessness is a regional problem

    Homelessness is a regional problem and encampment policies vary city by city, often causing unintended consequences on neighboring communities. What we also know is that stricter enforcement hasn't produced better results:

        Even under Oakland's new, tougher encampment policy (April 2026), the city does not cite or arrest people solely for camping. People who decline shelter can keep camping, and citations or arrests are avoided unless there's an imminent public-safety risk and shelter has been offered and declined.¹⁰

        Albany bans camping on city-owned property, but its own code says it won't enforce the ban against homeless people when no shelter is available.¹¹

        Fremont passed a citywide ban on camping, and its homeless population went up more than Berkeley's did.¹²

        San Jose has a policy to issue citations to those who refuse shelter, but only when the city actually has a bed to offer.¹³ Berkeley's policy allows citations in some cases even when no shelter is available.²

        San Francisco regularly arrests people for camping, but nearly 80% are released without being charged with a crime.⁸ Those who are charged and incarcerated cost taxpayers even more. 
A camping ban would do nothing to solve the Harrison Street lawsuit

While many people think a citywide camping ban would have prevented or resolved our current court case, that isn’t true.

The Harrison Street lawsuit (Berkeley Homeless Union v. City of Berkeley) is based on the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).⁵ A city ordinance can't override federal law.

Under Berkeley's current encampment policy, the city has cleared encampments that posed a public safety hazard, such as those in Ohlone Park.³ The Harrison lawsuit didn't strike down that policy. It added federal disability requirements to how the city carries it out, which is a big part of why clearing Harrison took so long. Most of the encampment was finally cleared in September.
What we CAN do

First, we need to prioritize public health and safety. When an encampment becomes an imminent danger, hazard, or nuisance, the city should intervene.

Second, we should invest in what works. City staff have said that Alternative Sites and motel-based shelters have been more successful than traditional shelters at moving people out of encampments and into permanent housing.¹⁴ While we need to be honest that there are some real roadblocks to implementation, I will work tirelessly to open a facility that gets people off the streets and out of the jail cycle.

The Alternative Sites model is based on the Grayson St. Shelter (2021 to 2022), a 50-bed indoor shelter with 40 spots for RVs to park. It was managed by Dorothy Day House and had running water, toilets, showers, storage, pets allowed, no curfew, case management, and up to $1,500 in vehicle repair help. It served about 150 people and connected about 30 to permanent housing.¹⁵

Two other programs that worked, the Mobile Crisis Team and Specialized Care Unit, provided non-police responses to mental health emergencies, but were cut in our recent budget crisis.  If elected, I promise no more cuts to behavioral health programs.

Third, we need to get creative with regional partners and mutual aid.

If elected, my office would launch a Homelessness Task Force. Modeled after the Sanctuary City Task Force,¹⁶ a Homelessness Task Force would have no budget or staff, but could bring together business, faith, and regional partners to coordinate creative solutions to fill service gaps.

subject: Housing
text:
I know Berkeley is a wonderful place to live, and I want to keep our city growing and welcoming new neighbors. We offer the strongest sanctuary laws, tenant rights, and labor protections in the county, and we should make those available to more people!

We need to invest in new housing of all types: affordable and subsidized housing, cooperative and land trust models, and market-rate, affordable-by-design building. We need to build housing for everyone in our community including students, seniors, and growing families. 

We need to protect the housing we already have. I support universal tenant protections, tenant unions, and pathways to ownership through the Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act (TOPA). I support investing in affordable family housing through the Small Sites program.

We need safe streets for all. Berkeley should be building infrastructure designed for a future with more cyclists, more transit, and denser communities. I support aligning and implementing our current streets studies.

We need to take care of our most vulnerable. The Harrison Street encampment is not safe or healthy for anyone, and we need to work hard as a city to respond. I support relocating unhoused residents to an alternative housing site with running water, sanitation, and wrap-around services. 

As we grow, we need to make sure our small businesses, city infrastructure, and affordability goals are able to keep up.

We need to invest in our small businesses, reduce vacant storefronts, cut permitting wait times and processing fees, invest in expanded open space and parklets, and help keep commercial spaces vibrant, clean, and full of art!

We need to support ‘Mom and Pop’ landlords by seeing them as partners in addressing the housing shortage. I'll work hard to provide resources, support, and guidance to make it as easy as possible to provide quality housing to our neighbors.

I'll also work to ‘Keep Berkeley Weird’! We need to support local creatives, build beautiful buildings, and offer outlets for activism, free speech, and self-expression. Berkeley can grow without losing what makes us special!

subject: Safety
text:
While our public safety debates so often become controversial, we all fundamentally want the same thing: to feel safe as we walk our streets, play in our parks, and bike to school.

We need to keep our services funded. Berkeley needs to keep our fire and police budgets solvent through the national municipal budget crisis caused by the Trump Administration. This includes raising revenue through Measures U and V and making sure we're appropriating effectively, taking care of our staff, and focusing on prevention.

We need to invest in crime prevention through design and policy. This includes urban lighting, afterschool and summer programming, and street diversion.

We need to hire the best people for the job. There are lots of types of city staff that can help us stay safe: mental health responders, street ambassadors, and civilian enforcement.

The Berkeley Police lead the country in de-escalation and non-violent response. This success is because of, and not despite, civilian oversight. We need to make sure our civil liberties are protected and our police are accountable.

We need to cancel our Flock contract. While the city has made good efforts to reduce the harm of Flock, there are other types of Automated License Plate Readers that do not threaten our civil liberties, and we should switch to those. Flock has shown a clear pattern of abuse and misuse, and no municipal privacy policy can protect us.

We need to respect the Police Accountability Board (PAB). After the murder of George Floyd, Berkeley voters approved the creation and funding of civilian oversight with over 80% of the vote. Over the last few years, the PAB has been systematically sidelined and ignored.

We need to keep our progressive use-of-force policies.  There has been an effort to roll back policies that restrict how much force police should use in different situations. Many of the policies have been in place for decades and play an important part in keeping our community safe.

subject: Budget
text:
Berkeley is in a structural budget crisis, and even if Berkeley voters approve both revenue ballot measures, the next council will need to manage further budgeting concerns. Budget cycles are never easy or predictable, but there are some things I will commit to:

I will keep our city workers involved in every step. We can't promise that no staff positions will ever be cut in the coming years, but we can keep our unions informed, involved, and empowered throughout the process. Our city workers know better than anyone what it takes to keep our services running, and their voices help us do our job.

I will plan for our future. We need to keep up with our long-term pension liabilities, deferred maintenance, and minimum staffing levels. We can hope future federal governments reverse the current cuts, but we can't take anything for granted.

I will engage the community. There are long-standing models of community budgeting that allow neighbors to come together and caucus and negotiate their priorities with real-world constraints. The more we involve and educate the public about the necessary trade-offs, the more effective our results will be.
