subject: Housing
text:
Berkeley should be a city where people at every stage of life can afford to live and where homelessness is addressed with compassion, accountability, and a focus on lasting solutions.

We need more housing at a range of income levels, especially affordable and workforce housing, while protecting existing homes, neighborhood character, and preventing displacement. As Berkeley grows, housing should be planned alongside the infrastructure, transportation, public services, and neighborhood investments needed to support it.

On homelessness, our goal should be moving people from the streets toward stable housing and connecting them with effective mental-health, substance-use, employment, and other supportive services. That requires stronger coordination with Alameda County and regional partners, effective outreach, transitional housing options, and clear standards that keep public spaces safe and accessible for everyone.

Success means more people housed, fewer people living unsheltered, and healthier neighborhoods for everyone.

subject: Safety
text:
Everyone deserves to feel safe in their neighborhood and to enjoy clean, welcoming, and accessible public spaces.

I support effective police, fire, and emergency response while also investing in prevention and addressing the everyday quality-of-life issues that affect residents and local businesses.

Public safety and civil liberties should go hand in hand. New technologies should have a clearly defined purpose, appropriate privacy protections, transparency, and public oversight. My approach is to identify the problem first, evaluate the options, listen to the people affected, and measure whether the solution is actually working.

subject: Infrastructure
text:
Berkeley needs to get the basics right: well-maintained streets and sidewalks, reliable infrastructure, safe transportation, accessible public spaces, and thoughtful long-term planning.

Our streets should work safely for people who walk, bike, drive, or take public transportation. Major projects should include meaningful community input and a clear understanding of costs, benefits, alternatives, and trade-offs.

As Berkeley grows, infrastructure must keep pace. Housing, transportation, climate resilience, neighborhood needs, and economic vitality should be planned together—not as separate issues.

That same approach should guide the future of our waterfront. I support protecting public access to the Marina while planning responsibly for the Pier, shoreline infrastructure, recreation, transportation, and climate resilience.

subject: Local Businesses
text:
Strong neighborhoods need thriving local businesses.

Berkeley should make it easier for small businesses to open, grow, and stay here. That means addressing unnecessary barriers, activating vacant storefronts, maintaining safe and welcoming commercial districts, and considering the needs of businesses and their customers when making decisions about development, transportation, parking, and public spaces.

Thoughtful growth can bring new housing, customers, investment, and vitality to our commercial corridors. But growth should come with the infrastructure and neighborhood investments needed to make it work.

subject: Accountability
text:
Residents deserve a City government that is transparent, accountable, and responsible with public dollars.

Berkeley faces significant financial and infrastructure challenges. We need to examine spending, staffing, contracts, revenues, long-term obligations, and operational efficiency while protecting essential services.

Before asking residents for more, City government should be able to clearly explain how existing resources are being used and what results they are producing. We should also aggressively pursue county, state, federal, and regional resources so Berkeley taxpayers are not carrying challenges that extend far beyond our city boundaries alone.

Good government also means listening before decisions are made. Residents should understand the costs, alternatives, and trade-offs behind major proposals and have meaningful opportunities to shape them.

I will bring the same approach to City Council that has guided my public service: listen carefully, bring people together, ask tough questions, and deliver results.

Listen. Connect. Deliver.

subject: Pitch
text:
About Ross

I’m a father, husband, and dedicated environmentalist. I’m running for Council to ensure a safer, greener, more affordable Berkeley.

I’ve spent the past fifteen years leading environmental efforts: I've worked on-the-ground restoring habitats in Haiti, I led teams monitoring urban tree canopy, I secured a deal that protected over 400,000 acres of forest on the East Coast, and I served on our local Sierra Club Executive Committee. It took me more than a decade to be able to afford to call Berkeley home. I’m running for City Council because I believe Berkeley can be the model of an affordable, well-run progressive city that delivers on its values.

As Councilmember, I will:

    Fight for more housing to bring down the cost of living

    Advocate for real solutions to homelessness

    Champion smoother, safer streets

    Support our first responders

    Enhance our parks and public spaces

    Grow our city’s economy and balance the budget

subject: Housing
text:
Berkeley's housing affordability crisis doesn’t just affect newcomers, but all of us: from parents and grandparents whose children and grandchildren can’t afford to live here, to businesses that can’t find workers, to those pushed out onto the street when rent goes up. While rents dipped slightly a couple years ago, they have started to climb again. We need to do more to bring down the cost of housing and protect low-income and long-term tenants in our community.

As Councilmember, I will: 

    Champion new housing at all income levels: from subsidized affordable housing for rent-burdened families and individuals, to permanent supportive housing to help folks struggling get off the street, to new market-rate housing that supports local businesses and grows our tax base, providing more revenue for better city services. 

    Support strong tenant protections, ensuring longtime residents aren’t driven out by rising prices or unfair landlord practices.

    Encourage family housing, “missing middle” housing like duplexes and quadplexes, and backyard cottages (accessory dwelling units) that make it easier for multigenerational households to stay together. 

    Support necessary zoning, building code, and other changes to make smaller, affordable-by-design homes more feasible to build, while ensuring we keep community benefits and strong design guidelines so that new buildings enhance our city. 

    Prioritize housing near transit and destinations like schools, jobs, and shops, helping to keep cars off the road and reduce our community’s environmental footprint.

subject: Homelessness
text:
Homelessness is one of the most visible, painful, and acute challenges facing 1. The status quo is not working. Everyone in Berkeley deserves to be treated with equal respect and compassion. We need to balance the needs of our unhoused neighbors with those of the broader community, especially where health and safety are concerned. Sleeping on the street isn't a compassionate situation for anyone, and the health risks of encampments affect encampment residents the most. We need to build real pathways back to stable, healthy lives, while also keeping our parks, sidewalks, and public spaces safe, clean, and welcoming for everyone. 

We cannot allow open-air encampments to become permanent fixtures in 1, which is why enforcement must be early and paired with regional RV sites, interim shelter, and shelter offers.

As Councilmember, I will:

    Fight to keep and restore funding for existing programs that are working. City-operated permanent supportive housing, such as the Hope Center, and the city’s RV buyback program are examples of existing programs that are working. Unfortunately, with the budget crisis, we're facing $3.5 million in cuts to the city’s Health, Housing, and Community Services. I will fight to increase revenue and restore funding to these essential city programs.

    Regional solutions to region-wide problems. The County has the funding, the shelter beds, and the case-management infrastructure for a truly regional response. We need to facilitate coordinated entry into the regional system that already exists, rather than trying to solve our regional homelessness crisis all on our own.

    Pair an RV and encampment ordinance with an inter-jurisdictional RV site, funded and operated by the County. I will be the champion for a competitive application for Alameda County Measure W (Home Together Fund) dollars and work with the County and neighboring cities on where to site it. For too long in Berkeley we have accepted an “anything goes” approach to unsheltered homelessness. This has placed an undue burden on residents, businesses, and visitors in West Berkeley. I will support policy and enforcement that will prevent encampments from forming in the first place.

    Fund permanent supportive housing. We must increase our permanent supportive housing capacity. This must be done throughout the city because 1 already hosts a disproportionate volume of homeless services compared to the rest of the city. These services will provide a pathway out of homelessness, rather than managing it indefinitely. We need market-rate housing projects to start breaking ground again to build our Housing Trust Fund back up, and we should put another affordable housing bond in front of voters now that Measure O funds have run out.

    Listen to city staff. In staff’s own words, "absent new sources of external funding… staff do not recommend opening new programs when several existing shelter programs face imminent risk of closure." I do not support adding new programs when budget cuts threaten our existing ones.

subject: Infrastructure
text:
Berkeleyans deserve world-class streets. That means not just smoother streets free of potholes, but also ones that are comfortable and welcoming for all road users, whether they're walking, biking, rolling, or driving. We especially need to ensure our streets are safe and accessible for the most vulnerable in our community, including children, seniors, and people with disabilities, both those who depend on automobiles for mobility, as well as those who can’t drive for health or safety reasons. Thanks to the generous support of Berkeley voters, Measure FF (passed in 2024) will provide some $270 million over 14 years to help fix our streets – but it’s up to the next City Council to ensure we use that funding efficiently and deliver on the street improvements Bekeleyans voted for. As your Councilmember, I will:

    Ensure Measure FF and City tax dollars are spent wisely and effectively towards fixing our streets, including repairing Berkeley’s failed streets, and ensuring new safety projects benefit all road users.

    Prioritize accessibility, mobility, and comfort for the most vulnerable among us, ensuring safety for people walking, biking, and using mobility devices, while preserving parking spaces for those who rely on them.

    Advocate for fixing broken sidewalks, support 1’s Equity Zone for priority paving, and support beautification and increased street trees on our neighborhood blocks and arterials.

subject: Safety
text:
Every family in 1 deserves to feel safe at home, walking to school, or out in their neighborhood at night. That means both safety from crime, as well as safety from abuse of power and technology. Real safety means more than just responding after something goes wrong; it means preventing harm in the first place. Keeping Berkeley residents safe requires balancing an effective police force with effective and responsible guardrails and oversight.

As Councilmember, I will:

    Ensure our police department has the resources to respond quickly and effectively to violent crime in our community, as well as the resources to deter and prevent crime before it happens.

    Support the Police Accountability Board’s role in providing independent civilian oversight and fair and impartial investigations.

    Require any policing technology to have clear and appropriate usage policies, including vendor requirements for data access controls, with enforceable mechanisms to hold bad actors accountable.  Flock does not meet these standards, and I would support moving off of Flock as quickly as possible.

    Support hiring of non-sworn first responders and civilian staff roles where feasible, ensuring our resources are utilized effectively. 

    Support community policing that builds real relationships and trust between officers and the neighborhoods they serve.

    Invest in lighting, visibility, and street design that help prevent crime before it happens.

    Balance accountability with compassion, so every resident, from small business owners to families to our most vulnerable neighbors, feels genuinely protected.

    Restore funding for a clinician-staffed, non-transport response unit for low-acuity medical calls, so engines and ambulances stay available for true emergencies.

    Fully staff our Emergency Communications Center, because alternative response only works when dispatchers have the capacity to send the right resource to the right call.

subject: Accountability
text:
Berkeleyans deserve world-class service from their local government, but our city has not always been a pinnacle of operational excellence. Our families and small businesses shouldn't have to choose between a city with the right values and a city where potholes get fixed, permits move quickly, and your tax dollars are spent effectively.

As Councilmember, I will:

    Provide rigorous budget oversight, ensuring every tax dollar is spent wisely and in line with the voters’ intent.

    Streamline permitting for housing and small businesses, so projects don't sit stuck in red tape for years.

    Support investments in the City’s operational efficiency, such as by modernizing outdated software and technology systems, to help deliver better services at lower costs. For example, the City should make it possible to auto-pay your waste collection bill.

    Prioritize constituent services, ensuring calls and emails are returned in a timely fashion, listening to diverse perspectives, and helping residents and local businesses get the assistance they need.

subject: Environment
text:
I've spent fifteen years working to protect the natural world, from restoring forests and wildlife habitat across the globe to serving on our local Sierra Club's executive committee. Berkeley's environment deserves that same care at home. Every family, in every neighborhood, deserves clean air, trees in their neighborhood, and a park nearby they're proud to bring their kids to. Protecting our local biodiversity, our creeks, our shoreline, and our urban forest is an important part of making 1 the vibrant, refreshing community that residents deserve.

As Councilmember, I will:

    Support planting more street trees, especially in the flatlands, to ensure every neighborhood benefits from shade and cleaner air.

    Keep our parks clean, well-maintained, and welcoming for families, kids, and seniors.

    Protect our shoreline and invest in the Berkeley Marina, preparing for sea level rise and supporting new transit options and Marina-focused businesses and activities..

    Turn Golden Gate Fields into a public park rich in amenities, while restoring wetland habitat and creating more access to the bay for everyone.

subject: Pitch
text:
I have spent my career designing clean energy policies and protecting low-income Californians. I know how to create policies that work.


With the commitment of Berkeley residents, we can have a vibrant, equitable, and sustainable city. I am your neighbor and a single mother in West Berkeley.  My daughter attends elementary school in the Berkeley Unified School District. Like many Berkeleyans, I am here because I love this city.

Berkeley is full of so much potential. Our city also faces serious challenges that are specific to this moment in history. Housing in Berkeley is largely unaffordable for people in low- and moderate- income brackets, seniors in our community cannot meet rising costs and face homelessness, and our city faces increasing budget deficits. While homicides are down in our city, traffic fatalities are up. Berkeley is quickly losing large portions of our black population.

​

And yet, we have everything we need, right here in our city, to address these challenges: we have a wealth of knowledge and resources, a collective commitment to equity and free speech, and systems that are capable of supporting us. I am running to work with you to help channel our community resources into meeting the challenges of our time, to provide equitable opportunities to those who pursue them, and to realize our great city’s exceptional potential.

subject: Pitch
text:
When I ran for City Council, I promised to be laser-focused on the most vital needs of our specifically — and the broader Berkeley community. I promised to be accessible, attentive, and collaborative. I promised to get things done that make life better for all of us.

 

Promises made, promises kept.

 

After two years on the City Council, my team and I have made major headway on some of the biggest issues impacting our district:

 

    We’ve reopened Civic Center Park as a public commons accessible to all;

    We’ve secured new housing at all income levels, including deeply affordable housing downtown;

    We’ve advanced significant pedestrian, bicyclist, and traffic safety improvements throughout 4; and

    We’ve made significant headway toward making Downtown a safe and accessible destination where small businesses, the arts, and community-serving institutions can thrive.

 

More than three dozen initiatives I’ve authored or co-authored are now codified in city law or are in the process of being implemented, and we’re just getting started. 

 

I’ve lived in Berkeley for more than 20 years, and I care deeply about this community. This November, I am running for re-election to continue the work we’ve started together. If you appreciate the stability, responsiveness, and focus I’ve brought to this office, if you want to continue to create a Downtown Berkeley that is thriving, inclusive, and more affordable, I humbly ask for your vote. Igor Tregub Priorities 

Elected in 2024, Councilmember Igor Tregub brings the experience we need, the dedication we deserve, and the progressive values we share.

​​

Igor is always working hard for you, and he is ready to continue his service on the City Council, creating positive change and fostering a more inclusive and equitable Berkeley for all.​

​

Igor's Priorities are Berkeley Priorities:

​

Build an Affordable Berkeley We Can All Call Home.

​

Both as our City Councilmember and as a twice-elected Berkeley Rent Stabilization Board member, I have championed every ballot measure to invest in affordable housing and to expand tenant protections. 

 

Using every available strategy and resource available, my top priority is to expand the dream of housing affordability and homeownership to Berkeleyans struggling to make it in our city. 

 

My efforts have resulted in Berkeley:

 

    Passing one of the strongest demolition ordinances in the nation to protect sitting renters;

    Opening up hundreds of units of new housing affordable to a wide range of income levels, including hundreds of affordable housing units in the Downtown; and

    Through an innovative small sites program that I championed both on and off the Council, keeping many seniors and families rooted in Berkeley rather than displaced.

​

Prioritize a Safe, Accessible, and Vibrant Downtown. 

​

The 4 Councilmember has the distinct honor and responsibility of representing Downtown Berkeley, the heart of our city. I have worked and continue to work with small business owners, city officials, and nonprofits to make our downtown the envy of the Bay Area. 

 

That requires smart approaches to public safety and a willingness to listen to impacted businesses. 

 

My vision: Downtown Berkeley should be an ever more inviting and welcoming destination for all, and it must sustain a vibrant art, cultural, and small business community.

 

I am working with diligence, focus, and attentiveness toward that goal. 

 

To that end, I have:

 

    Introduced dozens of policy items to cut red tape associated with permitting and reduce soft costs borne by small businesses; 

    Worked to improve lighting downtown to make our streets safer at night;

    Successfully ended an illegal dumping site in our downtown and continue to work with the city to address blight; and

    Continue to address the unacceptable commercial vacancy rate in our downtown. While this problem predates my time in office and is largely due to a variety of complex global and macroeconomic factors, for the first time in six years, it has declined to pre-pandemic levels.

 

Safe and Accessible Infrastructure. 

​

In my time in office, I have focused on making Berkeley streets safe for everyone, including seniors, people with disabilities, strollers, and rollers. 

 

My efforts have led to progress big and small, including:

 

    Reimagining Oxford Street as one that is safe for users of all modes of transit;

    Investing in safer pedestrian crossings and intersections throughout 4, and 

    Establishing a regulatory framework for the safe use of shared micromobility devices that does not impede access of our public sidewalks by pedestrians and wheelchair users. 

​

Vision Zero – a city where traffic accidents resulting in serious injury or fatality approaches zero – remains the goal, and we are making significant progress under my leadership.

​

Every day, I put my strong working relationships with leaders at BART and AC Transit on your behalf. I have been entrusted by my peers to serve as chair of the AC Transit Parcel Tax Oversight Committee, where I partner on more affordable, plentiful, and seamless ways to get around Berkeley and our region.

​

Help the unhoused rebuild their lives. 

​

My efforts have supported an overall reduction in Berkeley’s unsheltered homelessness population in recent years. However, far too many people are still living on the streets. This puts an enormous strain on the unhoused and our community. 

 

Helping our unhoused neighbors get off the streets and find stability remains one of my top priorities. 

 

Even before my time on the Council, my efforts to help build and finance the Hope Center on Berkeley Way, a revolutionary deeply affordable housing project with 60 beds and wraparound services, were key to its opening and continued service to our community.

​

In my two years on the Council, I've embraced a housing-first approach that has gotten close to 100 of our formerly unhoused neighbors off the streets and into supportive environments with wraparound services and treatment as needed. 

​

With a track record of building consensus to get things done, I continue to partner on a regional level with our neighbors to tackle the homelessness crisis from every direction.

​

I’ve worked to ensure that as many Measure W (a homelessness support ballot measure adopted in 2020) county dollars as possible go into addressing our homelessness crisis. I’ve been a relentless advocate in ensuring that Berkeley receives its fair share of Measure W dollars, because we have both a demonstrated need and the results to prove that our strategies are working to reduce homelessness in a strategic and compassionate way.

 

Champion Bold Climate Leadership. 

​

Berkeley has always led the way on the environment, often with my leadership. As a clean energy policy expert and Berkeley's representative to the Ava Community Energy Board (our clean energy community alternative to for-profit utilities), I have prioritized making Berkeley the first carbon-free city in the nation through successful efforts to reduce building emissions, expand public EV charging infrastructure, and invest in climate-resilient community gathering spaces, localized solar energy, battery storage, and community microgrids—with an emphasis on supporting renters with access to affordable renewable energy.

 

Our city’s climate leadership is something we should be proud of, and I bring the expertise needed to keep us on track.

​

​

There are no areas of city governance improvement that my efforts have not been instrumental in advancing. From ensuring a more accountable and transparent budgeting process, to relentlessly working to reduce red tape for our residents and small businesses, to standing strong with our immigrant communities, every day, in every way, I go to work on your behalf - for a Berkeley we can ALL call home.

subject: Policies
text:
You may have received a pamphlet from my opponent that is almost entirely devoted to tearing down my record of achievement on behalf of the people of Berkeley. It is full of misrepresentations. As the only candidate in this race with a history of public service to this community longer than nine months (the full extent of his record), I welcome the opportunity to set the record straight.
FLOCK

Berkeley’s Flock contract was first approved in 2023, before I joined the City Council. I not only voted against renewing Flock at the first opportunity, but worked with the Mayor and Councilmember Lunaparra to co-author and design the strongest possible set of privacy and civil rights guardrails against any use of surveillance. 

The 2025 vote my opponent references was a complicated sequence of votes that, thanks to my efforts, resulted in one of the strongest sets of guardrails in the nation concerning this technology. Notably, my opponent was not involved in these discussions at all. But for these efforts, Berkeley would have much weaker privacy and surveillance protections today. The real-world impacts of how data from this technology has been misused in other jurisdictions has become even more clear since the advent of the Trump Administration’s cruel and inhumane approach to immigration enforcement. In my votes at the Council, I have made it clear that no amount of safeguards is any longer sufficient given Flock’s abysmal track record with community trust as a vendor. I will continue to oppose contracting with Flock. 

I also voted against the lifting of a moratorium on the use of tear gas and was pleased to see a majority of the City Council agreed with me. I am proud to be the only candidate in this race who is endorsed by members of the Police Accountability Board, including its Chair and Vice Chair.
THE BUDGET

This council has had to make extraordinarily difficult choices in attempting to balance a nearly $30 million deficit. Through our due diligence, I was able to identify several million dollars per year in additional revenue that large corporations owed the City, which allowed me to work with the Mayor to reinstate several critical City positions and programs.

As Chair of the Health, Life Enrichment, Equity, and Community Committee and Council-appointed designee to Berkeley’s Behavioral Health Commission, I am working diligently to secure a sustainable funding stream that could help restore Berkeley’s mobile crisis center to handle calls that do not require police intervention.
SUPPORT FOR SMALL BUSINESSES

My opponent has challenged me on a 2024 item I co-sponsored to exempt the taxation of business gross receipts relating to government and philanthropic research and development grants in the public interest. As a UC Berkeley alumnus with a degree in Mechanical Engineering who has worked extensively with researchers at all three of the Bay Area’s major national laboratories, I saw time and time again how my colleagues, who had ideas of how to save our planet or produce the next life-saving medicine, had to move the small businesses they incubated out of Berkeley due to, among other things, locally-imposed financial constraints on their ability to continue growing them here. 

As your Downtown Berkeley councilmember I also know that keeping these small businesses here in Berkeley has a multiplier effect, as its employees frequent local retail, including downtown coffee shops, restaurants and other small businesses. I have taken a leading role in ensuring that our downtown becomes a safe, accessible, and vibrant destination for all and, among the other items I authored, making it easier for entrepreneurs and their employees to remain in Berkeley as a key strategy. Thanks to our collective efforts, the percentage of commercial vacancies in the downtown - which houses many early-stage companies developing these life-saving products - is down to pre-pandemic levels, and we’re just getting started.
HOMELESSNESS

The reasons why someone may fall into homelessness are complex and all too often intersect with economic inequality and all sorts of inequities that conservative national policies have fomented over many decades. Helping our unhoused neighbors rebuild their lives is not just a core campaign priority - it’s a mission to which I’ve devoted over two decades of my public service to Berkeley. 

Even before being elected to the Berkeley City Council, my efforts were instrumental in approving and securing funding for the Hope Center, a 60+ unit deeply affordable housing project with wraparound supportive services for those coming out of homelessness, while helping pass Measure O, a $135 million affordable housing bond, and Measure P in 2018, a ballot measure that has secured millions of dollars for homelessness services each year since then. (My opponent was not involved in any of these efforts, nor appears to have even voted in the November 2018 election in which Measure P was on the ballot).


In 2024, the fruit of these efforts became clear: Berkeley saw a 45% reduction in unsheltered homelessness. In my time on the City Council, I have built upon these efforts in a variety of ways - from working with the County Board of Supervisors to ensure that at least 80% of Alameda County Measure W (2020) dollars go towards homelessness services with an emphasis on funding new affordable housing and wraparound services in high-need jurisdictions such as Berkeley, to securing millions of dollars of state funding toward noncongregate supportive housing, including three projects that have opened up in or near 4 in the past two years. 

At the same time, I think most Berkeley voters understand that there are encampments and unhoused living situations that are fundamentally unsafe or uninhabitable for people sleeping there and/or unfair to other Berkeley residents going about their lives. I’m committed to continuing to be an effective change agent in helping our unhoused neighbors rebuild their lives in safe and supportive environments.
SUPPORT FOR THE ARTS

Ensuring that our downtown, and all of Berkeley, is a safe, accessible destination in which our arts and cultural uses can thrive is a top priority of mine. In my short time on the Council, I helped bring a pop-up art gallery at the former Half Price Books location on Shattuck and Addison, secured funding for catenary lighting in the Arts District, and am currently actively working with stakeholders to return the Aurora Theater back to its former home in Berkeley's Arts District. A significant amount of my attention has also focused on exploring various funding strategies to bring a movie theater back to Downtown. 

Regarding the specific project my opponent is referencing, I am limited in what I can say given legally privileged information that came before the Council prior to that 2024 vote - a difficult one for me - but part of the responsibility of a councilmember is also to take appropriate steps to avoid costly litigation that the city is unlikely to win.
HOPKINS

Hopkins Street provides an important access point for those who shop at Monterey Market and the other beloved small businesses along that corridor, attend Ruth Acty Elementary or King Middle School, or just go about their day. It is critical that this corridor is made safe and accessible to all - and that it is paved as soon as possible. 

As your councilmember, it is my duty to listen to the entire district, and opinions on the appropriate visions for Hopkins street safety improvements were split nearly down the middle. While I was disappointed that a supplemental referral by Councilmember Blackaby to also study alternative corridors such as Rose St and Ada St, which I voted for, did not receive the needed five votes to advance, I supported a study that would explore the feasibility of different approaches to make the Hopkins corridor safe and accessible for all, paired with a robust parking demand management system so that parking spaces are readily available to those who need to drive and park along the corridor. 

As I have been doing with other complex and contentious issues that come before the Council, I will hold a community listening session for 4 neighbors on whatever proposal might come before the Council in the future.
RENT CAPS

My opponent alleges that I voted for a less robust reduction in the absolute rent cap than a different proposal. Context and facts matter. The reality is I responsibly voted for the strongest rent cap that could actually pass. In 2024, the Berkeley City Council was voting to place Measure BB, which was later approved by the voters and is now law, on the ballot. In a public setting, a former member of the City Council stated that they would support a 5% absolute cap but not a lower one. Because they were expected to be the deciding vote on any tenant protection measure before council at that time, I cast a vote in support of this. 

Because of my vote, the measure received five votes - the minimum needed for the Council to adopt it - which is why we have a stronger set of tenant protections and a tenant’s rights to organize their building in place now. 

If I had taken the current position of my opponent on this issue (he was not involved in advocacy for or discussion on this issue at the time), these protections would not exist. I am proud to be the only candidate in this race to be endorsed by any current Rent Board members - let alone a supermajority of them - and the California Democratic Renters Council.
CEASEFIRE RESOLUTION

I worked with the Mayor and Councilmember Bartlett on a thoughtful ceasefire resolution that we felt could pass through this Council. We voted for it along with with Councilmember Lunaparra, one vote short of the needed five votes to advance, I voted for the only remaining resolution - one that spoke of our aspirations for peace and peaceful coexistence in that region of the Middle East, and continued condemnation of Islamophobia and antisemitism.
THE BOTTOM LINE

I have served this community for more than two decades – 2 years as a City Councilmember, 8 years as a Berkeley Rent Stabilization Commissioner, and many years of combined service on 12 city and regional commissions, 6 of them as their chair. 

My opponent can’t run on his record of public service to this community, because it barely exists. In fact, he can rarely be counted on to even vote! According to the voter file, he has not voted in five of the past six elections, choosing not to be counted as Berkeley voters have made major decisions on housing affordability, tenant protections, infrastructure investments, support for parks and public schools, and much more.

I welcome the opportunity to talk about our respective records. I know what I’ve accomplished for this community, and it would be nice to learn more about what my opponent has done, since he doesn’t have much to say about that. I know that I have the experience, the dedication, the progressive values, and the commitment to civic duty to help us navigate the challenging times ahead.

Yes, I have an extensive public record of service and have had to gain understanding, hear people on all sides, and make tough decisions on many difficult and divisive issues over the years. I work hard, strive to hear the diverse views of this community, and do my best to elevate Berkeley values in the decisions I make. In doing so, I recognize that reasonable people will disagree with some decisions I’ve made along the way. That’s ok! That’s Berkeley in action, and that’s democracy in action.

subject: Accomplishments
text:
A RECORD OF DELIVERING RESULTS FOR BERKELEY

​​In 2024, the voters of 4 elected Igor to serve as their Councilmember in a special election. With a 20+ -year record of community and public service—including eight years on the Berkeley Rent Stabilization Board and 12 local commission appointments—Igor brought decades of experience to City Hall and got to work delivering results. From expanding housing opportunities for people of all income levels while protecting renters to revitalizing Downtown, improving public safety, advancing climate action, supporting local businesses and workers, and making City Hall more effective and accountable, Igor has focused on turning community priorities into tangible results for Berkeley.

 

Igor is the experienced progressive leader who gets it done, and here are the results.

 

Many of these accomplishments require continued attention and followthrough. Igor excels at staying engaged and builds on this work in partnership with city staff, community, and the many stakeholders who make Berkeley such a vibrant and attractive place to be. 

​
BUILDING AN AFFORDABLE BERKELEY WE CAN ALL CALL HOME
​

✔️ Expanded deeply affordable housing downtown. Igor helped secure new housing at multiple income levels, including deeply affordable homes in Downtown Berkeley. Igor is especially proud of his leadership in securing funding and the vision for the Hope Center on Berkeley Way, a successful affordable housing project with 60 beds and wraparound services in Downtown Berkeley.

​​

✔️ Helped nearly 100 of our unhoused neighbors move into housing and supportive services. Under Igor’s leadership, Berkeley has continued a housing-first approach, connecting people experiencing homelessness with stable housing, wraparound services, and treatment when needed.

​​

✔️ Increased funding for affordable housing. Igor championed and campaigned for the successful Affordable Housing Bond and Large Landlord Windfall Profits Tax, generating hundreds of millions of dollars in additional revenue for Berkeley's Housing Trust Fund. Measure O alone generated $135 million of funding for affordable housing projects. As Chair of the Measure O Oversight Committee, Igor directed it towards a number of permanently affordable housing projects - some of which have opened and helped us welcome new neighbors.

​

✔️ Protected Berkeley renters from displacement. With Igor’s 20+ years of advocacy, he has been successful in strengthening renter protections, including helping craft and pass a Demolition Ordinance that has the strongest tenant measures in the nation. He also strengthened rent caps, advanced the Tenant’s Right to Organize measure, and ensured that the Small Sites Program, which helps keep seniors and families rooted in Berkeley, has necessary funding.

​

✔️ Approved thousands of new homes. In his two years on the Council and 12 years on the Zoning Adjustments Board, Igor voted to approve thousands of housing units across a range of affordability levels. Almost every affordable home built in Berkeley in the past 14 years and almost the entirety of our (affordable) Housing Trust Fund exist in part due to Igor’s leadership. Igor co-crafted and campaigned for instrumental affordable housing ballot Measures U1 (the Large Landlord Windfall Profits Tax), O (a $135million affordable housing bond), and P (funding for homelessness services and support).

​

✔️ Helped make homeownership more attainable. Igor helped craft a local density-bonus program encouraging the construction of lower-cost condominium homes, built consensus on the council to unlock new affordable homeownership opportunities, and streamlined approval of Accessory Dwelling Units.

​

✔️ Made thousands of Berkeley homes safer. Igor secured changes to key programs and ordinances, such as Berkeley's Seismic Safety Ordinance, the Rental Housing Safety Program, and the Exterior Elevated Elements Inspection Program, ensuring that thousands of renters live in safe and habitable housing.

​
REVITALIZING OUR DOWNTOWN
 

✔️ Reopened Civic Center Park as a public commons. Igor helped restore the park as a safe, welcoming public space accessible to everyone, strengthening Downtown as a welcoming place to gather and connect.

​

✔️ Helped bring Downtown's commercial vacancy rate back to pre-pandemic levels. Igor advanced dozens of policies to reduce permitting red tape and lower the costs of opening and operating a small business, while working diligently and methodically to address prolonged commercial vacancies by cultivating a variety of vibrant storefronts and creative, arts, maker, pop-up, and community-serving uses. And he’s just getting started!

​

✔️ Helped local businesses stay open and thrive. Igor worked with small businesses and City staff to secure permits, remove barriers, and connect businesses with resources they need to succeed. This is a core component of Igor’s constituent services. 

​

✔️ Brought more arts and culture to Downtown. Igor helped secure a pop-up art gallery at the former Half Price Books location on Shattuck and Addison, secured funding for catenary lighting in the Arts District, and is currently actively working with stakeholders to bring the Aurora Theater back to its former home in Berkeley's Arts District. A significant amount of Igor’s attention has also focused on exploring various funding strategies to bring a movie theater back to Downtown.

​​

✔️ Invested in a more vibrant, walkable Downtown. Igor helped advance attractive placemaking projects on Addison St., Oxford St., and Harold Way to create safer, more attractive spaces that encourage neighbors and visitors to make Downtown Berkeley their place to gather, shop, and spend time with family and friends. 

​​
IMPROVING PUBLIC SAFETY AND ACCESSIBILITY
​

✔️ Made Berkeley streets safer and more accessible. Igor advanced pedestrian, bicycle, and traffic-safety improvements throughout 4, with a focus on safety for people walking, biking, using mobility devices, pushing strollers, and taking transit. A number of crosswalk improvements and traffic calming measures are underway or have been completed thanks to his leadership.

​

✔️ Made sidewalks safer for everyone. Igor authored reforms to Berkeley's shared micromobility regulations to improve safety, protect ADA accessibility, and strengthen accountability when scooter and e-bike operators do not follow the rules of the road.

​​

✔️ Reimagined Oxford Street for safer travel. Igor championed, advanced, and secured funding for the initiative to make Oxford safer for people walking, biking, using mobility devices, and taking transit. He continues to work with the City and the University to support safer pedestrian access and crossings.

​

✔️ Improved lighting in Downtown and around campus. Igor helped secure better lighting in high-traffic areas to make our streets and public spaces safer and help deter crime.

​

✔️ Strengthened regional transportation partnerships. Igor worked with BART and AC Transit to advance more affordable, accessible, and seamless transportation options, including serving as chair of the AC Transit Parcel Tax Oversight Committee.

​

✔️ Strengthened public safety and police accountability. Igor worked with community members and the City Council to advance Berkeley's Reimagining Public Safety package, including a Police Accountability Board with strong oversight powers. 

​

✔️ Stood up to Flock and supported our immigrant communities. Igor consistently voted and spoke out against Flock. While Igor was in the minority on this vote, his work did succeed in strengthening Berkeley's codified privacy and surveillance protections. He helped advance a strong sanctuary city policy that reaffirmed the City’s commitment to supporting and protecting our immigrant communities - and helped codify it into law.

​​
AN ACCESSIBLE, ACCOUNTABLE, AND RESPONSIVE GOVERNMENT
​

✔️ Has made your government work for you. Igor’s 4 Council office has resolved hundreds of constituent cases, ranging from infrastructure, pedestrian, and traffic safety improvements to resolving illegal dumping and noise complaint cases on behalf of neighbors like you.

​

✔️ Cut red tape. Igor is diligently working to reduce red tape associated with permitting - whether it’s a group of neighbors organizing a block party, a small business making Downtown Berkeley its home, or a beloved community event seeking timely approval. Making Berkeley government operate efficiently and effectively, while being welcoming and responsive to our community, remains both a policy priority and a focus of his day-to-day work.

​

✔️ Effectively addressed Berkeley’s budgetary challenges. Igor worked with his colleagues and the City Administration on a new framework with a full accounting of Berkeley’s short-term budgetary revenues, costs, and liabilities. Despite a challenging nearly-$30 million budget deficit that Igor helped close, Igor was able to find additional short- and long-term funding solutions and make the city’s cuts less painful than they otherwise could have been. He is already hard at work on next year’s budget to ensure that the city continues on the path of spending only what it can afford while identifying sustainable sources of revenue that focus on corporations paying their fair share. Protecting services that help our most vulnerable neighbors remains a top priority as we weather challenging national and local economic conditions.

​

✔️ Championed a responsive, accountable, transparent, and data-driven government. Igor is working with colleagues to establish clearer budget criteria that identify quantifiable goals and metrics as money is distributed. Igor has also championed council initiatives establishing a proactive communication system to alert the community of upcoming infrastructure projects from Public Works, EBMUD, PG&E, and other large housing or commercial development projects. He is also working to ensure that the University of California is in closer contact with the city and neighbors to mitigate disruptions prior to large capital projects in 4. Igor is working every day to drive forward a data-driven city that is responsive and accountable to you. 

​

✔️ Established responsible rules for artificial intelligence (AI). Igor helped craft several items to promote transparency, human oversight, civil rights protections, and consideration of workforce impacts as the City adopts new technology. He co-authored a proposal for one of the first municipal responsible use of AI regulations in the nation, which is now in the process of implementation.

​

✔️ Put residents—not corporations—at the center of Berkeley elections. Igor helped pass Berkeley's public financing program and other reforms designed to reduce the influence of corporate money in local politics.

​

✔️ Turned creative ideas into policy through effective partnerships. More than three dozen initiatives Igor authored or co-authored in just over two years are now codified in Berkeley law or are actively being implemented.

​
STRENGTHENING COMMUNITY WELLNESS & QUALITY OF LIFE
​

✔️ Invested in Berkeley's community and cultural life. Igor supported funding for local nonprofits, cultural programs, public events, and community-engagement initiatives, including helping bring together several events to Downtown Berkeley for the first time - including Make Music Day and the Downtown Berkeley Pride Fest.

​

✔️ Fought to restore mobile mental-health crisis services. As a member of the Behavioral Health Commission and chair of the Council's Health, Life Enrichment, Equity, and Community Policy Committee, Igor is working with City and County partners to identify funding to restore mobile crisis response and strengthen services for people experiencing nonviolent mental-health crises.

​

CONTINUING BERKELEY'S CLIMATE LEADERSHIP

​

✔️ Helped make Berkeley a national climate leader. Igor helped craft the nation's first building electrification ordinance as well as a revolutionary Building Emissions Savings Ordinance - models subsequently replicated by hundreds of jurisdictions nationwide.

​

✔️ Secured millions of dollars for affordable and clean transportation opportunities. As a Member of the Ava Community Energy Board (our clean energy community alternative to for-profit utilities), Igor successfully amended an Ava Community Energy motion to invest an additional $3 million in its e-bike pilot—$1 million above the staff recommendation—funding rebates for approximately 2,400 additional e-bikes and e-trikes.

​

✔️ Advanced neighborhood climate resilience. Igor helped advance partnerships to bring community resiliency centers to Berkeley neighborhoods while supporting localized solar, battery storage, and community microgrids—with a focus on access for renters.

​

✔️ Fought pollution and held polluters accountable. Igor championed policies supporting zero-emission appliances, residential solar, and utility accountability, while working to defeat legislation that would have made solar-equipped housing more expensive.

​

✔️ Kept Berkeley's building electrification leadership moving forward. After a federal court overturned Berkeley's landmark building electrification ordinance, Igor advanced new green-building reach codes to continue reducing building emissions and improving indoor air quality.

​

✔️ Building a just, clean-energy economy, Igor helped advance Berkeley Green New Deal workforce initiatives and a Just and Equitable Transition program designed to create pathways to stable, middle-class careers as Berkeley moves away from polluting industries.

​

✔️Took on large corporate polluters. Igor has a long history of taking on large corporations on behalf of the public - whether it’s fighting a proposal to ship coal through our communities, calling on oil and gas companies to pay their fair share for the environmental harms they caused, or combatting the investor-owned utility monopoly.

​​

✔️Promoted small business clean energy incentives. Igor continues to partner with state and regional agencies to expand cost savings and incentives for green infrastructure for local small businesses.

​
 EXPANDING WORKER PROTECTIONS
​

✔️ Raised labor standards for Berkeley workers. Igor helped advance stronger worker protections through increases to Berkeley's minimum wage, a Fair Workweek policy, one of the first sweatshop-free procurement ordinances in the nation, and other local labor standards. These initiatives help make Berkeley a more affordable place to live for Berkeley residents.

​

✔️ Made good jobs part of Berkeley's development strategy. Igor worked with the Alameda County Building Trades Council to develop the Hard Hats Ordinance, encouraging major construction projects to use local hire, project labor agreements, health care, and other high-road workforce practices. He is also leading efforts to adopt state legislation that would codify these protections.

​

✔️ Protected workers during the clean-energy transition. Igor helped craft and pass a strong local Just and Equitable Transition program supporting workers in existing polluting industries while Berkeley moves toward a cleaner economy.

​
A LIFETIME OF SERVICE
​

✔️ Showed up for our immigrant neighbors. As an immigrant, Igor is actively involved with several mutual aid and foot patrol initiatives and has spearheaded a number of Know Your Rights forums and walks to downtown Berkeley businesses, so that everyone has the tools to keep their employees and customers safe. 

​

✔️ Showed up for Berkeley neighbors during the pandemic. Igor worked with Mutual Aid to personally deliver groceries and meals to Berkeley seniors when they needed support most.

​

✔️ Made service a lifelong commitment. From local boards and commissions to statewide advocacy and hands-on volunteer work, Igor has spent decades putting his time, expertise, and energy to work for our community.

subject: Platform
text:
Housing people can afford to keep. Public space everyone can use. Services people can rely on.

I have lived in Southside since 2016, first as a transfer and re-entry student and now as a renter, organizer, and medical case manager. I have seen how quickly a housing problem can become a health problem, how public space supports daily care and community life, and how a blocked sidewalk or unanswered service request can make an ordinary day harder.

Southside is growing. New housing, institutional expansion, construction, and increasing street use are changing the neighborhood. That growth creates public responsibilities. People need homes they can afford, places where they can gather without paying for entry, and public systems capable of serving a denser neighborhood.

My platform brings those responsibilities together. Berkeley should add homes while helping existing residents remain, protect and rebuild the places that support public life, and fund the infrastructure and services that growth requires.
Three Plans, One Governing Standard

Each part of this platform follows the same standard: identify the need, assign responsibility, determine how the work will be funded, and report what residents actually received.

A policy announcement is only the beginning. Residents should be able to distinguish what was requested, approved, funded, delivered, and maintained. When something is delayed, the public should know which decision, institution, or resource is holding it up. These three plans depend on one another.

Housing without preservation can displace the people growth was supposed to serve. Housing without public space leaves residents with fewer places to rest, gather, and build community. Housing and public space without maintenance leave the neighborhood with facilities that exist on paper but cannot be relied upon.

The same connection works in the other direction. Stable housing helps people maintain relationships and participate in neighborhood life. Public spaces give care networks, culture, recreation, and emergency preparation somewhere to operate. Dependable City services keep homes, streets, and gathering places accessible and usable.

That is the governing standard I will bring to Council: growth should expand Berkeley’s capacity to house people, support public life, and provide dependable services.
What Residents Will Be Able to Track

Residents should be able to see:

    Homes approved, completed, occupied, preserved, and lost

    Affordability levels, tenant outcomes, and ownership opportunities

    Public land and usable public space gained, restricted, or lost

    Restrooms, water, seating, shade, trees, rooms, and accessible routes added or repaired

    Service requests, response times, repeat failures, and permanent repairs

    Community-care connections, crisis-response coverage, and documented service gaps

    City, UC, developer, and project-sponsor commitments completed or delayed

    Capital costs, recurring operating expenses, and responsible funding sources

Public reporting should show where conditions improved, where they did not, and what decision comes next.

subject: Housing
text:
Berkeley needs more homes. It also needs to preserve existing lower-cost housing, prevent displacement, and expand homes that remain affordable permanently.

My Housing Stability Plan connects production with preservation. It calls for earlier assistance when a renter receives an eviction notice, a social-housing and preservation partnership, clearer housing-delivery procedures, stronger public and community ownership, and public reporting from application through occupancy.

The plan also asks UC Berkeley to account for enrollment, campus housing, property acquisitions, repair needs, and the effects its decisions have on the surrounding rental market. Major development should identify the sidewalks, sewers, transit, sanitation, trees, public space, and emergency access it requires.

The public measure is whether Berkeley adds homes while giving current residents a stronger chance to remain.

subject: Infrastructure
text:
Public space gives community life somewhere to happen. A shared meal needs a location. A neighborhood meeting needs an accessible room. Rest requires seating, shade, water, sanitation, and enough time to remain.

My Public Space Plan begins with an inventory of the land, rooms, restrooms, gardens, trees, seating, drinking water, emergency locations, and accessible routes Southside already has. It then identifies what is missing, who controls possible sites, what public-access rights exist, and what maintenance each place requires.

The plan seeks more indoor and outdoor gathering places, durable public-access agreements, responsible operating budgets, a Southside tree and amenities plan, and early identification of land that could be protected or acquired for public use. It also calls for restoring People’s Park as public land, ecological space, and a place for community life while pursuing affordable and supportive housing on appropriate alternative sites.

The public measure is whether Southside gains durable places where people can gather, rest, meet daily needs, and belong without paying for entry.

subject: Services
text:
Maintenance is governance. A service request should begin a process with a responsible department, an expected next step, and a way to verify whether the underlying problem was resolved.

My City Services Plan calls for service-resolution standards, coordinated accessible-route repairs, and annual planning for predictable conditions such as move-in, move-out, waste collection, construction, loading, and shared scooters obstructing sidewalks and curb ramps.

It also proposes a Southside Community Care Network connecting City and County services with campus programs, health providers, student organizations, cooperatives, businesses, faith communities, neighborhood groups, and mutual-aid organizations. The City and UC should provide dependable services and resources. Community networks should help people find support, maintain relationships across student turnover, and identify needs that public systems are failing to meet.

Emergency preparation, major development, and UC projects belong in the same service framework. Each should identify accessible routes, transportation effects, sanitation, emergency access, maintenance duties, funding, and the institution responsible for delivery.

The public measure is whether an ordinary problem gets fixed, care reaches the person who needs it, and the improvement continues working.

subject: Pitch
text:
My name is Syrak Micael. I was born, raised, and educated in Berkeley, graduating from UC Berkeley with degrees in Economics and Public Policy in December 2025. Now, I’m running for Berkeley City Council to represent students and longtime residents of 7, which includes the UC Berkeley campus and most of our Southside neighborhood. As an organizer and student advocate, I’m deeply committed to making the city more affordable and accessible to  students and marginalized community members. 

Growing up in Berkeley, I worked to support and empower my community. Surrounded by activists, I became involved in efforts within the Eritrean diaspora, where I raised awareness about our community and its experiences, spoke up for human rights and accountability, and advocated for services and support for Eritrean refugees and those seeking asylum when they arrived in the East Bay. My parents immigrated here during the Eritrean war for independence, and my passion for supporting those in need in Berkeley continues to be inspired by my family’s history and culture. 

As a teenager, my community engagement expanded. To lift up the next generation, I mentored youth as a soccer coach for Eastshore Alliance FC. My Berkeley High peers and I held a sit-in at the Berkeley Police Department Headquarters in support of the Black Lives Matter movement in 2020. While studying at Berkeley City College, I was an Umoja Student Leader. I advocated for spaces for underserved Black students, facilitated the reopening of the Umoja village, and tutored my peers in calculus and statistics.

At UC Berkeley, I continued to collaborate alongside marginalized students as an organizer and advocate. In 2024, I was elected as the Transfer Student Representative in the Associated Students of the University of California (ASUC). I worked closely with transfer and non-traditional students to work toward creation of re-entry themed student housing and write grants for better lighting across University Village. As a Berkeley student, I partnered with others to make significant institutional change as a member of the “Black Triad” (African American Student Development, Black Student Union, and Black Recruitment and Retention Center),  Cal Young Democratic Socialists of America, Cal Berkeley Democrats, and the Berkeley Student Food Collective. During my last semester at Cal, I connected students to local politics: as a Campus Organizer intern with the Alameda Labor Council, I led the UC Berkeley registration and “Get Out the Vote” campaign for Prop 50. My leadership of student-centered campaigns for change expanded my commitment to making sustainable change in my hometown.

  Credit: Introvert/Wikimedia Commons

In my current position as a Housing Advisory Commissioner for the City of Berkeley, I’ve voted to hold landlords accountable, fund improved housing infrastructure, support affordable housing development, and renovate existing affordable housing. 

My track record of creating and sustaining change is visible in my communities, on campus, and in the city. As your 7 Councilmember, I will continue to advocate for students and underserved community members. I strongly believe that housing is a human right, that living should be affordable, and that everyone should feel safe in our city. I will continue the fight for affordable housing, a lower cost of living, and a safe and inclusive Berkeley that we are proud to call home.

I can’t make change on the Council without your support! 
If you want to help build a student-powered campaign in Berkeley, donate or sign up to volunteer. 

To learn more about my platform, check out our detailed issues here. Stay up to date with our campaign by following me on Instagram, Bluesky, and TikTok (@syrakforsouthside).

subject: Housing
text:
Addressing Berkeley’s affordable housing crisis requires both strong tenant protections and real investments in housing that keeps students and long-term residents in the city. Throughout my work in the Associated Students of the University of California, I have never been afraid to push the University when students' needs are at stake, and I have built strong partnerships while advocating for the quality of life of transfer and non-traditional students. As a councilmember, I will use those relationships and that experience to work with partners inside and outside the UC system to advance meaningful solutions for affordable student housing in Berkeley and across the state. I will:

    Invest in seismic safety for Berkeley Student Cooperative housing, which is facing $20 million in mandated renovations paid for by tenants due to its proximity to the Hayward Fault Line

    Institute a vacant commercial property fee in conjunction with the existing vacant residential property fee and/or a temp process for businesses and direct the revenue to affordable housing and rehabilitation of existing units

    Leverage D7 transit-rich zones near AC Transit and BART corridors that comply with SB 79 as sites for future meaningful development

    Allocate dedicated Berkeley Housing Trust Fund predevelopment loans for D7 non-profit projects and establish an Affordable Housing and Sustainable Communities (AHSC) Task Force to strategically pair the D7 housing proposals with transit investments

    Launch a public transparency dashboard managed by our office to track housing project timelines, funding allocations, and affordability levels with clear safeguards to prevent luxury-only development

    Unionize Resident Assistants (RAs) to demand equitable payment for their labor and better housing conditions

    Support stronger demolition controls, protect and expand Berkeley’s Just Cause for Eviction Ordinance, and extend the Berkeley Tenant Protections and Right to Organize Act

    Advance an updated citywide economic analysis to better understand the current drivers of displacement, housing insecurity, commercial vacancy, and development feasibility

subject: Safety
text:
I believe that public safety in Berkeley should be grounded in community trust, transparency, and solutions that address the root causes of harm rather than in punitive approaches with limited long-term success. Our community cannot rely on the Berkeley Police Department. A safe 7 and City of Berkeley is one where our residents, students, and local businesses feel supported through public health responses, accountable policing, and public spaces designed for community well-being. Safety policy is incomplete without safeguards on civil liberties, upholding and reinforcing Berkeley’s commitment to sanctuary, and empowering community organizations to be partners in stewarding a safer city for everyone, especially our most vulnerable neighbors.

    Transition to a car-free Telegraph to improve pedestrian safety, boost local businesses, and create a safe community third space

    Oppose mass surveillance and protect data security through auditing and oversight for existing and potential contracts with any third-party 
    entity that does not keep City information safe

    Support students’ and community members’ right to protest and organize, with blocks on BPD access to military-grade weapons

    Envision sanctuary city status as an ongoing commitment that requires clear policy, enforcement, and zero tolerance for ICE collaboration

    Integrate restorative justice practices to facilitate an anti-carceral approach to safety in the community

    Protect pedestrian and bike mobility during construction projects to prevent accidents and injuries for our neighbors

    Revitalize the Dwight Triangle as a community third space for community to gather, organize, and enjoy

subject: Labor
text:
As someone who has grown up in Berkeley my whole life, I understand that a thriving 7 is built on the dignity of its workers and the strength of its unions and small businesses as pillars of the community. When wages are fair, workers have the power to organize, and local businesses can grow with a fighting chance; the entire community benefits from this investment. Our collective strength and size as a population translates to soft power that can be leveraged to advocate for better conditions and quality of life. Ensuring that residents can meet their basic needs – from food to healthcare to stable housing – requires policies that strengthen worker protections and expand access to essential resources. I will treat economic stability for working people and students as a foundation for a healthy and resilient Berkeley community. 

    Expand relationships with community and campus partners with weekly Office Hours to ensure students and residents have consistent access to nutritious food through community gardens, primary care referrals, mental health resources, and essential services 

    Introduce legacy business grants and lease protections to reduce barriers and costs for locally owned businesses in high-rent corridors like Telegraph, stabilizing storefronts and sustaining the neighborhood institutions that generations have relied on and are fundamental to Berkeley history

    Require large employers and developers receiving city incentives to meet living-wage standards and demonstrate meaningful local hiring commitments, ensuring jobs for D7 residents, and supporting the One Fair Wage campaign in Alameda County of 30 by 30 ($30/hr by 2030: if your business has over 25 employees, then you need a minimum wage of $30)

    Support worker-led organizing at the UC, including the Save Science Bond Measure which would strengthen union jobs at the University of California as well as expand scientific research for lifesaving cures

subject: Pitch
text:
I’m Councilmember Mark Humbert
I’m excited to announce that I’m running for re-election!

It has been a privilege and a pleasure to serve you and all of my neighbors in 8 these past four years, and I hope to serve 8 and Berkeley for another four years. Together, we’ve accomplished a lot:

Fighting to protect local shops and successfully persuading the Planning Commission to limit Elmwood rezoning to just three sites

Enhancing 8 parks and replacing the Willard Clubhouse with a new, award-winning facility

Passing Measure FF to fund smoother, safer streets

Supporting our first responders with superb chiefs, new tech, and wildfire preparedness

Adopting Middle Housing zoning to enable the creation of smaller, more affordable homes

Supporting the Elmwood Music Festival, Russell Street Halloween, Berkeley Sun Day, and other community events and organizations

And more!

I would be honored to earn your vote again. 

I have lived in Berkeley for over 25 years and I feel privileged to have served our City as the 8 Councilmember for nearly four years now. Berkeley has been a wonderful place to live and raise my family, and I want to continue to give back to our community so that others and their kids can enjoy the same opportunities I did.

As your Councilmember, I have prioritized support for our basic City services and infrastructure, as well as planning for our future. If I have the honor of being reelected for another four years, I intend to maintain this pragmatic and focused approach.

 

I believe that serving our City and our values demands that we prioritize basic services and infrastructure, especially in lean budget times. I believe in giving Berkeley’s excellent City workers the support (and breathing room) they need to focus on keeping residents safe and healthy, and our roads and civic facilities in the best shape possible.

If elected for another four years, I will stay squarely focused on making sure the things we value most come first, and that City resources are allocated efficiently and consistent with our values.

subject: Accomplishments
text:
A record of getting things done for 8 — from safer streets and restored bus service to smart housing policy that protects the neighborhoods we love. Select any item to read the details.
Expand All
Collapse All
Persuaded the Planning Commission to protect local shops by adopting his "tailored zoning" approach

At a City Council work-session in November 2025, Councilmember Humbert was the first and only Councilmember to speak up in favor of focusing new housing on just three sites in order to protect local shops.

Over the next six months, Mark worked with three fellow Councilmembers to promote his tailored zoning approach and get the Planning Commission on board. In May 2026, the Planning Commission voted in support of his approach, focusing zoning for new homes on limited parcels, not just in the Elmwood, but on other commercial corridors as well. Learn more about Mark's approach to new homes in Elmwood here. And for even more in-depth information, check out his Housing FAQ
Shepherded the now-open and award-winning Willard Clubhouse and Park improvements through final Council approval

Initiated by former Councilmember Lori Droste, Mark brought the Willard Clubhouse and Park improvements over the finish line, navigating tense, last-minute zoning considerations to deliver the final Council vote in support of the project. The old Willard clubhouse was inadequately sized and lacked essential facilities for afterschool care and neighborhood events.

Thanks to Mark and Lori's efforts, it has now been rebuilt as an award-winning, highly sustainable community space. Mark fought to ensure the project was not delayed or watered down, so it could serve as many of our kids and neighbors as possible.
Championed “quick build” safety improvements for Claremont Avenue to reduce speeding and improve safety for people walking, biking, and driving

Claremont Avenue has long been a dangerous roadway, frequently used by people speeding through between freeways. In response to the most recent tragic loss of life along this roadway, Mark engaged with the community and City staff to develop and kick off a plan for “quick build” safety improvements.

These low-cost strategies represent low-hanging fruit for improving roadway safety by encouraging drivers to slow down and be more aware of their surroundings. These quick-build solutions are currently under construction and serve as a precursor to more extensive long-term improvements anticipated along Claremont Avenue following Alameda County flood control projects beginning later this year or next.
Successfully persuaded AC Transit to restore bus service on Ashby Avenue

During the pandemic, AC Transit eliminated bus service along Ashby Avenue. Mark was instrumental in persuading AC Transit to bring back an Ashby bus line as the agency considered which services to restore after lockdown. AC Transit was prepared to leave Ashby Avenue without service and instead bring back bus lines elsewhere.

By carefully analyzing AC Transit ridership data, Mark was able to show that the Ashby segment of the prior Line 7 was the more logical and cost-effective choice for restoration. The AC Transit board agreed, and Ashby once again has bus service in the form of Line 27.
Brokered the Council compromise on middle housing to bring medium-density, naturally affordable homes to more Berkeley neighborhoods

Also first initiated by former Councilmember Droste, Berkeley's Middle Housing efforts aim to promote the creation of new homes in modestly sized projects in Berkeley neighborhoods that previously had exclusionary zoning. This effort culminated in final Planning Commission and Council votes during Mark's time in office.

Faced with competing proposals — one of which would have created fewer homes than we need, and one which would have effectively eliminated certain density limits entirely — Mark helped find the middle path for Middle Housing. He helped broker the deal from the dais that led to a consensus proposal winning broad approval from the Council.
Eliminated duplicative reporting for police equipment use and led the charge to permanently appoint Berkeley’s Chief of Police

Due to changes in State law, police reporting procedures previously adopted by the City Council were creating duplicative and conflicting requirements. Mark introduced the Council item that streamlined and consolidated these reporting requirements, so the Council and public would still get the information they need — but in a single report that comports with State law.
Advanced community engagement and design work for safety improvements to Zachary’s Corner and earmarked money for improvements from UC settlement funds

As a member of the UC/City/Student relations committee, Councilmember Humbert fought for UC Berkeley settlement funds to be set aside for the design and construction of safety improvements at Zachary's Corner. Seventeen years ago, this dangerous intersection at Warring and Derby was the site of the tragic loss of five-year-old Zachary Cruz to traffic violence.

Intersection changes to slow down vehicles and improve sight lines have been a long time coming, and Mark insisted that UC settlement funds be prioritized for this project. As a result, community meetings have taken place and a new design has been selected, with construction anticipated to take place soon.
Funded the Music in the Elmwood Festival, Russell Street Halloween, and Berkeley Sun Day with funds from his office budget

Mark deeply values the community events that bring our neighborhood together. That is why he has reliably provided funding to key community events including Russell Street Halloween, the Music in the Elmwood festival, and the nascent Berkeley Sun Day festival.

Mark has given $1,000 annually from his Council office budget to Russell Street Halloween. And when City bodies declined the Elmwood business association's request for an arts grant, Mark stepped in to provide $7,000 in rescue funds for the Music in the Elmwood festival. Mark is deeply committed to running a lean Council office that leaves room for critical funding for community events.
Introduced an item to reform Berkeley’s byzantine rules for hot tub installation

After a routine hot tub installation resulted in a lengthy neighbor battle and Council hearing, Mark took action to ensure that such disputes do not routinely bubble up to the City Council. Mark introduced an item to have City planning staff develop revisions to Berkeley's Zoning Ordinance that would standardize and streamline the rules and processes for obtaining permits for new hot tubs. This seemingly small change reduces staff time and costs, and aligns Berkeley with how other cities adjudicate Jacuzzis.
Fought for fairness and flexibility for ADU and duplex owners

Across multiple efforts to increase regulatory burdens, Mark has fought for basic fairness and flexibility for mom-and-pop landlords who own duplexes or ADUs and live on site with their tenants. Although Mark is broadly supportive of basic tenant protections — especially for those in large and corporate-owned apartment buildings — he recognizes and fights for the idea that the relationship is fundamentally different when you are sharing your home or property with your tenant.

Mark has repeatedly resisted efforts to place onerous requirements on small landlords that could force them to live long-term with problematic tenants. And Mark was the sole vote on the City Council against rules (now overturned by the courts) that would have made it hard for small landlords to determine fair market rents for their units.
Lobbied state legislators to include Berkeley in pilot programs for speed enforcement cameras

Automated cameras for speed enforcement are a no-brainer for improving safety on Berkeley streets. Unfortunately, the California State legislature has continued to limit their use and failed to expand pilot programs to include Berkeley (or simply all cities across California). When the speed enforcement camera pilot program came before the State legislature, Mark introduced an urgency item to have the City Council urge state legislators to include Berkeley in the pilot. Although the state still has not done so, this continues to be an area of advocacy for Mark.
Initiated study of 4-way stop improvements for key intersections

Following a series of serious accidents at Berkeley intersections that featured only two-way stops, Mark introduced an item referring to staff a study of improvements at key intersections to slow traffic, increase safety, and pursue newer, more flexible standards for the installation of four-way stop signs.
Requested full funding for the City 50/50 sidewalk repair program
