Under State law, property owners are responsible for repairing sidewalks next to their property; however, the City of Berkeley's 50/50 program splits these costs with property owners to incentivize sidewalk repairs. Unfortunately, this program has been underfunded for years, resulting in long backlogs and poor sidewalk conditions.

Early in his tenure, Mark put forward a budget referral to fully fund this program and speed up repairs. Although the full Council did not ultimately prioritize this expenditure, Mark's goal of fully funding this program has found its way into recent ballot and bond measures.

subject: Zoning
text:
I believe that we can protect what makes Elmwood and Berkeley great while also living up to Berkeley values of being an inclusive community that welcomes immigrants and creates the homes our kids will need to build their own families and lives in Berkeley.

Here’s the short version:

    California law requires Berkeley to zone for at least 9,000 new homes from 2023–2031
    California fair housing laws also require Berkeley to allow for new homes along commercial corridors in high-resource areas, like College Avenue
    The initial proposal would have rezoned all College Avenue shops
    I personally met multiple times with neighbors and leadership of Save Berkeley Shops, and I took their well-founded concerns to heart
    In November 2025 I put forward the “tailored zoning” approach that protects our local shops, and focuses the rezoning on just three high-opportunity sites: the 7-11, the Wells Fargo parking lot, and the Post Office parcel. This rezoning would allow, but not require, the owners of those sites to propose new homes.
    From November 2025 to May 2026 I worked hard to build support on the Planning Commission and among as many councilmembers as I could legally work with
    In May 2026 the Planning Commission voted to recommend my tailored zoning approach, not just for Elmwood, but also North Shattuck and Solano. It will now go before the full City Council so the rest of my colleagues can discuss and, I hope, approve this targeted zoning change that meets our obligations under State law.

Here’s the long version (see the dedicated page for even more depth):

California State law requires Berkeley to make good on the policies in its Housing Element and to affirmatively further fair housing. This means allowing for new homes along commercial corridors in high-resource areas of Berkeley in a way that is equitable with what has been allowed in other areas of town. If we fail to do so, it is possible Berkeley could not only lose funding for affordable and supportive housing, but also lose control of our local zoning through the “builder’s remedy.” If that happened, there would be little limit to the height of what could be proposed and the protections I’ve been fighting for would be in jeopardy.

My Solution

Happily, I believe we can actually achieve a win-win in Elmwood: Allowing for more homes on targeted, underutilized parcels while preserving the unbroken, pedestrian-oriented retail fabric that makes it unique. That’s why I’m continuing to push hard for my “Tailored Zoning” approach that would focus rezoning on the 7-11, the parking lot behind Wells Fargo, and the Post Office site (if USPS leaves).

We are in a fortunate position: these sites are currently dominated by parking lots and are not significantly contributing to the walkable feel of Elmwood. They also happen to be the three sites that City staff and consultants identified as being the three most feasible for new housing. We can therefore rezone just these three sites, achieve almost the same capacity for new homes that was originally projected for a broader rezone, protect existing retail, and enhance the neighborhood and add more foot traffic for our local shops.

I have championed this Tailored Zoning approach for nearly a year, and I’m very pleased that the Planning Commission has voted decisively in favor of it—though there is one site they changed that I intend to push to fix when it comes to Council. Right now we are waiting for final work on the new zoning to complete and for it to come back before Council, possibly in the late fall. I will work hard to land the Tailored Zoning approach, and I think I’m uniquely positioned to try to get a majority of my Council colleagues on board.
Correcting Misinformation

I must, unfortunately, also address misinformation that I’ve heard circulating in the neighborhood: Neither the City nor I are seeking to “bulldoze” Elmwood shops; and the Elmwood theater is already a protected landmark that I have fought and will continue to fight to protect. I have been a booster for the Elmwood theater, and when the Elmwood Theater’s big premiere of Oppenheimer was threatened by damage from a car accident, I personally worked with City staff to ensure the theater could reopen on time. Keeping in place the existing landmark that already protects the theater is non-negotiable.

If you would like to read in a lot more detail about the Corridors Zoning Update and housing in general, please check out my CZU FAQ and my dedicated Elmwood Zoning page.

subject: Surveillance
text:
Here’s the short version:

I support giving BPD the right tools for the job, while also applying rules and oversight to safeguard civil liberties and make sure our data are protected and used appropriately. I will continue to insist that any vendor the City uses be held to a very high and strict standard.
Here’s the long version:

I want to be candid about this because I feel that Berkeley faces a difficult balancing act and there are multiple things I believe are true:

    Done right, automated license plate readers (ALPRs) are an effective tool to solve and prevent crimes and which help our police department cope with having fewer officers;
    I do not trust Flock because they’ve had multiple instances of carelessness (at best) with other cities’ data;
    Other providers are even less transparent about their practices and are perhaps even more entangled with the Trump administration than Flock; and 
    If Berkeley continues using ALPRs, we need an airtight contract with strong data protections, and which we can instantly exit at will and without penalty, regardless of who operates them.

Berkeley and California already have strong prohibitions against sharing ALPR data with federal agencies. This is the legal bare minimum and absolutely non-negotiable. The City is currently engaging in an RFP process to seek alternatives to Flock’s ALPRs.

For me, additional red-line requirements for any future ALPR contract are: strict City control of who can access Berkeley’s data; thorough and regular auditing of who has access and who is searching for what; and, most importantly, contract escape clauses that let the City cancel the contract at any time, for any reason, and with no financial penalty for the City.

Having seen first hand how quick and effective these devices are at catching stolen and crime-associated vehicles coming into Berkeley, I’m convinced that they offer significant public safety benefits. And with strict data controls and contract provisions, I believe Berkeley can make use of ALPRs while respecting civil liberties and protecting the public from abuse of these systems. And if we have any reason whatsoever to suspect abuse, we can pull the plug.

subject: Willard Pool
text:
Like many of you, I deeply miss Willard Pool and wish we could bring it back. South Berkeley has a dearth of public recreation facilities, and the closure of Willard Pool made this scarcity that much worse. Unfortunately, the City Council has few if any tools to resurrect Willard Pool.

Following the defeat of Measure C in 2012, which would have provided bond money to renovate and re-open the pool, the Berkeley Unified School moved on from the idea of having a pool there. BUSD continues to own the property, and my understanding is that they have not expressed interest in selling it to the City or bringing back a pool at that location.

My sense is that the School is hoping to someday use all or a portion of the site for a new auditorium at Willard Middle School, which currently only has a less-than-ideal “cafetorium.” Decisions regarding Willard Pool thus rest fundamentally with BUSD, not the City Council. I would welcome a citizen’s initiative provide funding and encourage BUSD to reopen the pool and/or sell the property to the City (this would have the advantage of a lower approval threshold than a Council-initiated measure). But, unfortunately, given BUSD’s current plans and the 2012 defeat of Measure C, the City has not been able to prioritize this versus other easier infrastructure wins.

subject: Pitch
text:
Berkeley is central to my story.

My parents — a Lebanese mother and Finnish father — met as graduate students at the International House. Born in Oakland, they brought me home as a newborn to a small apartment on Dwight Way. Soon after, we moved near Lawrence Hall, where my two sisters arrived. My mother worked as a librarian for the City of Berkeley and for the Berkeley public schools, and my father was a scientist and lecturer at Cal. Lacking any extended family in the U.S., our immediate neighbors and local community became my family.

I attended all of Berkeley's public schools, community college, and UC Berkeley, earning a degree in Electrical Engineering, Computer Science, and Material Science. While in college, I worked as a lab tech in downtown Berkeley and in the restaurant industry. Since graduating, I have helped found Berkeley-based startups and worked in big tech.

Today, my wife — a first-generation Mexican-American from East Oakland — and I are raising our two children on Panoramic Hill. We care for my mother-in-law in our home, while my mother and stepdad live near Monterey Market. Caring for this community is deeply personal to me.
Why I'm Running

Berkeley needs better.

For years, we have endured long and uncoordinated road and sidewalk closures, blocks of vacant storefronts, littered streets, failing infrastructure, unbalanced budgets, and leadership that is out of touch with local realities.

Despite adding thousands of housing units, rents remain high; meanwhile, BART and AC Transit ridership, along with school enrollment, have all declined. While our leaders promised a car-free future supported by bikes and transit, the reality is a wave of ride-share and delivery drivers, sidewalks cluttered with electric scooters, crumbling roads, and a decade of development that has failed to lower costs in any meaningful way.

To build an equitable and vibrant Berkeley, we must reject this trajectory. The city needs representatives who understand new AI technologies, who rely on verified data for decision-making, who listen to their constituents, who can create local jobs, and who speak out against injustice, wherever it may lie. If you support this vision for our future, I ask for your vote.

subject: Platform
text:
Big ideas for all of Berkeley

These reach beyond 8. They're long shots that would take real partnership to pull off — and they'd make the whole city better.
Universal After School Care

Fund onsite after school care at every BUSD elementary school, so every family has a safe, enriching place for their kids until the workday ends — no waitlists, no scramble across town.
Reintroduce Trade Programs at BHS

Bring hands-on career and technical education back to Berkeley High — shop, construction, automotive, electrical — so students can graduate straight into an apprenticeship or a good union job, not only a four-year degree.
Reopen the University's Public Spaces

Work with UC Berkeley to give the community back spaces it has lost over the years — starting with Cal's turf fields, which could host neighborhood sports, leagues, and events when the teams aren't using them.
Bring Back Willard Pool

Restore and staff Willard Pool so it can once again offer swim lessons, lap swimming, and low-impact exercise for Berkeley residents of every age.
Save Alta Bates Medical Center

Sutter plans to move Alta Bates' emergency room and hospital beds to Emeryville, leaving Berkeley without a full-service hospital. Keep acute care here by putting every creative option on the table — a partnership with UC, a voter-backed healthcare district, or a new operator for the Ashby campus.
More Parks for a Growing Berkeley

More homes, more people, more students — and our parks have to grow with them. Put parks in the infrastructure equation alongside roads and sewers: plan new open space with every wave of housing, and turn underused lots and street space into pocket parks and playgrounds.

subject: Pitch
text:
Over the last 10 years, the voices of Berkeleyans have been drowned out by outside special interest groups and lobbyists, who have infiltrated our neighborhoods, co-opted leadership, deceived voters and divided our communities.

During the last election, optics and gatekeeping politics undermined our opportunity for a significant change of course in a number of districts, without which we would be in a better place than we are now.

We have to do more than simply speak out against injustice. We have to actively change the policies and systemic structures that feed off of inequity, greed and power, undermining every level of decision-making that follows.

Join me in creating the kind of fundamental core shifts in our policies and politics that put our needs and the sustainability of our community first and Take Berkeley Back for Berkeley!

subject: Housing
text:
Housing is a Human Right

Over the past decade, our neighborhoods have become the victim of a new wave of displacement, sold to us through the so-called “housing crisis.” Rising costs and manipulated markets have created a global push to commodify housing, which is gentrifying neighborhoods, pushing out homeowners and destroying communities while lining the pockets of real estate corporations, housing industries and development.

Politicians have become complicit in creating the irresponsible over-densification of our neighborhoods through legislation from our Senate and Assembly, which is being exacerbated by current City Council members who are doubling down on the current levels of upzoning. This is threatening small businesses and posing a detriment to the stability of our neighborhoods without providing the affordable and accessible housing that we need.

In order to create truly affordable housing, we must put regulations in place that stop the inflation of market rates and end density bonuses and extractive giveaways to developers. We must require steep community benefits working with impact investment partners who want to change the landscape of investment by uplifting our communities. We must challenge state policies that put unjust, unsustainable and environmentally unsafe demands on the construction of housing, driven by speculation and predatory capitalism. Housing is a human right, not a commodity.

Through my work in the community and as a Housing Advisory Commission representative, I worked with others to create tenant protections and bring back displaced neighbors through the creation of Berkeley’s housing preference policy. However, this is only one small step. We have to do more. 

Support for small sites is another step that Berkeley has taken to address access and availability to housing.  If we combine these efforts with the implementation of a rent freeze, the repeal of the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act and a re-imagining of how we create and define “affordable” in the first place, we can reshape how our housing policies are being confined by the current status quo.

subject: Small Businesses
text:
Small businesses are the heart of our neighborhoods. My connection to Elmwood and other small business districts that are under threat, such as North Shattuck and Solano, span not only my lifetime of growing up in Berkeley, but also my children’s.

 

Fallout from the building of massively dense developments and the elimination of parking is taking away customer access to our beloved small businesses owners, many of which we have already closed. Yes in My Backyard (YIMBY) and climate lobbies have joined forces to demonize responsible growth and use double talk to disguise their agendas as grounded in equity and accessibility when, in fact, they’re funnelling money, extracting assets and mining resources while causing displacement and blight in thriving neighborhood spaces.

 

Berkeley is too small for obvious tactics like these to undermine its functionality. So how do we keep getting a City Council whose majority somehow keeps selling us out? It’s because Berkeley has permitted an insidious political culture, where electeds are influenced to ignore their personal wisdom and power and succumb to the poison of political “negotiating” instead of standing firm in their core values and moral obligation to do right by all residents.

subject: Policing
text: We must invest in community services, not over-policing and intrusive surveillance, particularly of our minority residents because black and brown lives do matter as much as any others; provide shelter, housing stability and social services, including mental health and workforce training; and cut the overspending on police, which does not necessarily equal a decrease in crime.

subject: Infrastructure
text: We must re-address emergency response time and the effects of “road calming” obstructions to emergency vehicles, as well as “equitable safe streets” and “quick build” designs, which are removing parking for small businesses and access to elders and disabled residents.
